events.title: AI 'kill switch' may need to be mandatory, Anthropic co-founder tells BBC
events.summary: AI "more powerful by the day", Anthropic co-founder tells BBC An artificial intelligence "kill switch" which can be checked by a third party may need to be mandatory for companies, a co-founder of one of the world's largest AI firms has told the BBC. Jack Clark, one of seven founders of Anthropic, said a way of shutting off AI software completely if it gets too dangerous was something society "might want to eventually pass rules around". Clark said "most labs have different ways of being able to pull the plug", including Anthropic, but said lawmakers may need to enforce having one. AI's rapid development and fears over the risks it poses to humanity have been thrust into the spotlight by a series of warnings from executives and staff at AI firms. Some have said publicly there is a chance the technology could, if unchecked, kill all humans. Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei over the weekend called for the pace of AI development to slow and be more closely monitored, as the company has done before, though some have questioned the motivations behind this. Amodei added that any action to rein in AI development should be done "without sacrificing commercial advantage". AI staff 'genuinely frightened' for humanity's future, ex-Anthropic researcher tells BBC Published 2 days ago Clark told the BBC that specifics around "kill switch" requirements and verification should be part of "the larger policy conversation" taking place around AI. "Should you mandate for companies to definitely have a kill switch? Is that kill switch verifiable by a third party?" he asked. "I think that's the kind of thing society is going to want to know and might want to eventually pass rules around." Anthropic, which was formed in 2021 by a group of former employees of its rival OpenAI, is currently at the centre of a debate around AI safety. Last week, a post from an artificial intelligence researcher who quit Anthropic over concerns AI could wipe out humanity went viral. In response, Anthropic scientist Evan Hubinger said he personally thought the possibility of human extinction from AI was ">10% within the next decade" . Computer scientist and Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton, known as the "Godfather of AI", told the BBC on Friday that a 10% chance of AI killing all humans was "not unreasonable" , external . He and others with similar concerns have suggested AI could do so by taking control of important systems connected to the internet and turning them on humans. However, some in the AI industry have suggested the fears around it destroying humanity are overstated or may be designed to generate hype. Clement Delangue, leader of the developer platform Hugging Face which was hacked by OpenAI bots, said last week: "Sorry, but asking Jacob [Coxon] about AI extinction risk is like asking your AC guy about climate change." "Not saying it's necessarily uninteresting or wrong per se but let's keep things in perspective." George Arison, the leader of Grindr, said the fears going around AI tools were being used by the companies to support their business plans. Anthropic, which was valued at $965bn (£713bn), is preparing for an initial public offering on the stock market, allowing people to buy shares in its firm. OpenAI, which was most recently valued at $852bn (£630bn), had been expected to do the same, but OpenAI's Altman said on Friday this would not happen this year due to the current debate around AI safety. Arison said: "The only way to justify these valuations is to actually claim: 'I'm going to take over every industry and I'm going to take over every job, and my AI is going to be doing all that work.'" Asked what percentage he would put on all humans being killed by AI, Clark said: "I don't think these statistics are that useful", but added that allowing AI to continue as a "totally unregulated industry" was a bad idea. "We are rolling dice with immense risks," Clark said. "And the point is, we have to change the course of this industry." UK government rejects 'kill switch' idea for dangerous AI Published 4 days ago US lawmakers have put forward legislation dubbed the Kill Switch Act that would require companies to have a way to shut down problematic AI tools. It would also give certain government agencies the power to demand a tool be turned off or limited. However, US President Donald Trump has rejected calls to slow the development of AI, saying on social media "AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX". Trump later compared fears to concerns over the "Global Warming Scam of not so long ago, where everyone was going to die from extreme heat". In an earlier post, he wrote: "There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!" In the UK, the government has recently rejected the idea of creating a kill switch , with a spokesperson saying it "would not prevent them being developed or misused elsewhere".

events.title: Abbott to pay $489m to settle infant formula allegations
events.summary: The Abbott recall underscored broader concerns about the safety and oversight of the US infant formula supply. WASHINGTON – Abbott Laboratories, the maker of the popular infant formula Similac, will pay nearly US$385 million (S$489 million) to settle claims that it knowingly sold formula manufactured in facilities that did not meet safety requirements. The settlement, announced on Sept 14 by the US Justice Department, follows years of scrutiny of a plant Abbott managed in Sturgis, Michigan, that produced a sizeable share of the nation’s formula supply. In 2022, Abbott initiated a recall of powdered formulas manufactured at the plant, after federal health officials linked the products to four infants who were hospitalised with rare bacterial infections, two of whom died. Production at the facility was halted, contributing to a nationwide formula shortage that lasted for months . In a statement provided to The New York Times on Sept 14, the company, which did not admit liability or fault in the settlement, noted that “no unopened, distributed Abbott infant formulas have ever tested positive” for the bacteria that sickened the babies, including containers from the homes of the infants. “We make infant formula with the same care we would for our own families and are deeply committed to earning and maintaining caregivers’ trust,” the company said. The federal government’s complaint detailed unsanitary conditions at the Michigan plant, including roof leaks, deteriorating equipment and inadequate cleaning procedures. Instead of fixing the roof leaks, the department said, Abbott installed umbrellas, which diverted water from production areas but created a wet environment ripe for bacterial growth. The company’s spray dryers, which were used to turn liquid formula into powder, had cracks and pits, which increased the risk of contamination, the complaint said, and Abbott ran more batches of formula through the dryers between cleaning cycles than was safe. The US Justice Department also claimed that Abbott purposefully chose not to test for bacterial contamination and that, when the company did perform tests, it did not share positive results with the Food and Drug Administration. In a 2022 consent decree reached with the Justice Department, Abbott agreed to replace the plant’s roof, address sanitation protocols and take other corrective steps, though it did not admit liability. In a hearing before a House panel that year, an Abbott representative said it prioritised “safety and compliance in our plants”. In 2025, the formula company ByHeart, whose products were linked to an infant botulism outbreak, shut down its Pennsylvania plant after inspectors found safety violations, including mould in a clean-water tank and dead insects in a production area. The company recalled all lots of its formula. Nearly US$349 million of the Abbott settlement funds will go to the federal government and just over US$36 million will go to state Medicaid and the federal supplemental nutrition programme for women, infants and children, known as WIC, that purchased Abbott’s formula. Three whistle-blowers who first filed complaints about the plant will receive US$69 million. NYTIMES This article originally appeared in The New York Times .

events.title: China targets offshore operations of brokerages in crackdown on pay loopholes, corruption
events.summary: The move extends Beijing’s regulatory reach to financial institutions’ overseas activities, which have been a grey zone for corruption China’s securities regulator and its industry body are moving to close compensation loopholes for brokerage management and staff, extending anti-corruption oversight to overseas operations for the first time, as Beijing pushes the sector to build world-class investment banks. The Securities Association of China, a self-regulatory body under the supervision of the regulator, recently sent brokerages a revised draft of its rules on “clean practices”, seeking industry feedback by September 29, domestic media reported on Monday, citing industry sources. Under the proposed rules, offshore operations have been explicitly targeted for integrity oversight, marking a major expansion of Beijing’s regulatory reach into financial institutions’ overseas activities – a sector long viewed as a grey zone vulnerable to illicit transfers and kickbacks. Brokerages will be required to establish clawback mechanisms to recover bonuses and performance pay from employees who violate ethical standards or regulatory rules. Brokerages must also prepare an annual report on integrity management and have it reviewed by their board.

events.title: Thune sees role for Congress on AI — Trump does not
events.summary: Majority Leader John Thune is asserting Congress' prerogative to act on AI — but he's urging a "light touch" even in the face of "consequential risks." Why it matters: On his first day back after a five-week break, Thune (R-S.D.) outlined his vision for congressional action on an issue President Trump has dismissed as a " hoax ." "Congress has a job to do," Thune said. "I think there are some potential consequential risks associated with AI," Thune told reporters when asked if he believes AI poses an existential threat to humanity. He added, "Guardrails there make sense to me" about cutting-edge, frontier AI models. But Thune also said that "there are always people who are creating a worst-case-scenario-type conversation out there." Driving the news: An AI panic is rippling through Congress, but mostly on the Democratic side, with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) calling to "slow down the pace of development" of AI to avoid a potentially catastrophic outcome. Publicly, Trump is professing not to be concerned and insists that he should have the sole authority to regulate AI. "The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades," he posted on his Truth Social account Monday morning. Zoom out: Republicans aren't questioning Trump's ability to lead the country's approach to AI regulation, but they are suggesting that Congress has a role to play. And they aren't ruling out legislation. "So we may need to do something," Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said. "But there are existing guardrails, and corporate responsibility is a big part of this." Zoom in: Thune said he spoke with Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) on Saturday night about their AI bill, which would force companies creating frontier AI models to guard against catastrophic risks and submit to federal oversight. Thune said he has been working with Commerce Chair Ted Cruz (R-Tex.) to reintroduce the bill "hopefully soon." House GOP leaders, meanwhile, have given no indication they plan to keep the chamber in session after this week to work on AI-related legislation. "I don't know that staying in more weeks in September is going to be the catalyst for that," Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.), the lead Republican on the FRONTIER Act , told Axios. Between the lines: Before this weekend, much of the AI debate in Washington — and in Senate races — was focused on data centers and the amount of electricity they consume. Republicans, as well as the White House, are eager to prove to voters that they won't face higher utility bills caused by data centers and their need for megawatts. Thune left open the possibility of the Senate voting on a version of the House's Ratepayer Protection Act, which is aimed at ensuring communities are not forced to pay more for increased energy use by data centers. The House is expected to vote on the bill Tuesday. What we're hearing: Thune is uniquely prepared for the AI discussion, having worked on AI legislation for years. Before he joined leadership, he chaired the Commerce Committee, which has jurisdiction over AI. His familiarity with the complicated and evolving subject comes in contrast to many lawmakers who have little experience with AI. Johnson even said on a podcast he has never used an AI chatbot. "Congress is not the expert on this subject because we are not in the frontier labs with them," he told reporters Monday evening. The bottom line: Thune is signaling he's open to some regulation that wouldn't stifle innovation. "I think you also want to make sure that the more advanced threats can be mitigated," he told reporters. "I do think we are in a race with China, and I think there's huge upside, obviously, with AI as well."

events.title: Trump's $5,000 checks get chilly Senate GOP reception
events.summary: Data: OMB ; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Visuals Senate Republicans are doubtful — and, in some cases, dismissive — of President Trump's proposal to give Americans $5,000 checks if Republicans keep control of Congress. Why it matters: Trump's proposal isn't dead on arrival. But Republicans aren't exactly lining up behind it either. "I am withholding judgment on the bill until I see their list of pay-fors," Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) said. "I don't support going and borrowing $1.2 trillion to be able to write the checks." "I would need to see details on it," Sen. Ted Budd (R-N.C.) said. Sen. Steve Daines (R-Mont.) said he wasn't sure about the mechanics of the proposal but that he's "also worrying about $40 trillion in debt." "You know, there's no specific proposal out there," Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) said. "And obviously, however that were to come together, Congress would have a big role in determining." Zoom in: There are two massive unknowns about the " Trump Dividend " that the president promised in Dallas last week: eligibility and price tag. Vice President Vance has suggested that wealthy Americans wouldn't receive the payment. If every "every adult citizen in the United States" were eligible, as Trump suggested, it could cost some $1.3 trillion. That would be more than three times what the U.S. collects annually from tariffs and other customs duties and fees. The intrigue: Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.), who frequently defers to Trump, said Sunday that Congress would have to approve the payments. Asked in NBC's "Meet the Press" if he'd commit that the checks will be sent, Johnson said, "I commit that Congress will work through it and find consensus on that like they have to do everything else." Rep. Keith Self (R-Texas) told Axios: "Well, if it happens, I'm recommending to people that they put it away in order to pay for the additional inflation. We will see." — Axios' Kate Santaliz contributed reporting for this story.

events.title: I got paid $5,000 to move to a place I'd never heard of
events.summary: Brianna Beyrouti says moving to a cheaper part of the US means she can afford to take her kids on holiday Published 15 September 2026, 00:08 BST When Brianna Beyrouti looks back on her former life in the city of Portland, Oregon, she says she had been financially "drowning". "I was absolutely living paycheque to paycheque. Every time the smallest thing came up, it was like 'Oh, gosh, the kids need shoes, how am I going to afford that?' As a single parent, everything falls on my shoulders." Last year, Brianna left Portland and its metropolitan population of 2.5 million people. She and her two children moved 2,000 miles east to Muncie, Indiana, a small city with 65,000 people, a university and lots of open space, taking advantage of a scheme that contributed $5,000 towards the cost of the move to boost population growth. The relocation has been a revelation for her finances. She continues to work remotely for the same bank, so her annual salary of $107,000 (£79,000) is unchanged, but she has been able to buy a home for the first time. And her mortgage is less than she used to have to pay in rent. In Portland she was paying rent of $1,290 a month for an apartment, while the combined cost of her mortgage, home insurance and property tax for her detached home in Muncie is $1,100. Add the fact that state income tax is lower in Indiana, and that her car insurance and energy bills have also fallen, and Brianna says she is $600 a month better off. "I'm able to live my life more than I was before," she says. "When my kids want something, I'm much more inclined to say yes. My quality of life has increased dramatically." Brianna and her children swapped Portland for Muncie Brianna is not alone in swapping a big city for a smaller one. As the high cost of living continues to bite in the US, many of the biggest cities are seeing their populations fall, as people leave in search of cheaper property. A 2025 report from the National Association of Realtors found that for people moving to a different state, affordability was their primary reason. , external As a result, big cities from the likes of New York and Los Angeles to Portland, Oregon have seen a dip in their populations , external in recent years, further fuelled by the greatly increased acceptance of remote working since the Covid-19 pandemic. By contrast, some small towns and cities across the US, such as Muncie, are seeing their populations rise after decades of decline. The number of people who live in Muncie hit 65,466 last year, official figures showed. , external This is up from 65,194 in 2020, but still way down on its population of 71,828 in 1990. To help it stand out from the crowd, and encourage remote workers to move there from outside Indiana, Muncie's local council offers them $5,000 in cash to cover their relocation costs. It does this via a website called MakeMyMove, which lists several such relocation support schemes offered by similar small cities and towns across the US. These pay MakeMyMove a subscription fee. Other incentives locations offer potential new residents are complementary cinema tickets, restaurant vouchers, and even free bottles of wine. Brianna and her children are one of around 100 families to have moved to Muncie through the MakeMyMove programme. She says she hadn't heard of the city before. Across the US, MakeMyMove says it helped 1,000 people in total relocate last year, and is on target to increase that to 1,500 in 2026. Moving to Jacksonville, Illinois has allowed Elena Chrysostomou to buy a home Scientist Elena Chrysostomou also used a relocation support scheme to swap a big city for a small town. In 2024 she relocated from San Diego, California, to Jacksonville, a town of 17,700 people in rural Illinois. The move was backed by the Jacksonville Regional Economic Development Corporation (JREDC), which gave her $5,000 in cash, plus a "quality of life package" worth $4,000 that includes free gym memberships and golf passes. The JREDC says that while the region is "already a great place to live", the support scheme helps to "sweeten the deal". Elena was spending $3,000 renting a one-bedroom apartment in San Diego, but she now owns a three-bedroom home, with a mortgage of $1,868. At the same time, her salary has gone up 22% after she changed jobs, and her commute has gone down from a 15-minute drive to one of just one minute. "I never thought that I'd be able to afford a house on my own, I always thought I'd need a partner, and even then, in San Diego, it would be so tough," she says. "It's just more freeing. There's more security and independence." While both she and Brianna have no regrets, they do admit to some drawbacks to their new lives. These include the narrower range of activities and restaurant choices, leaving behind friends and family, and for Brianna the difficulty of settling her children into new schools. And while in Portland Brianna enjoyed walking to parks and shops, she now relies on her car to get anywhere.

events.title: I got paid $5,000 to move to a place I'd never heard of
events.summary: Brianna Beyrouti says moving to a cheaper part of the US means she can afford to take her kids on holiday Published 15 September 2026, 00:08 BST When Brianna Beyrouti looks back on her former life in the city of Portland, Oregon, she says she had been financially "drowning". "I was absolutely living paycheque to paycheque. Every time the smallest thing came up, it was like 'Oh, gosh, the kids need shoes, how am I going to afford that?' As a single parent, everything falls on my shoulders." Last year, Brianna left Portland and its metropolitan population of 2.5 million people. She and her two children moved 2,000 miles east to Muncie, Indiana, a small city with 65,000 people, a university and lots of open space, taking advantage of a scheme that contributed $5,000 towards the cost of the move to boost population growth. The relocation has been a revelation for her finances. She continues to work remotely for the same bank, so her annual salary of $107,000 (£79,000) is unchanged, but she has been able to buy a home for the first time. And her mortgage is less than she used to have to pay in rent. In Portland she was paying rent of $1,290 a month for an apartment, while the combined cost of her mortgage, home insurance and property tax for her detached home in Muncie is $1,100. Add the fact that state income tax is lower in Indiana, and that her car insurance and energy bills have also fallen, and Brianna says she is $600 a month better off. "I'm able to live my life more than I was before," she says. "When my kids want something, I'm much more inclined to say yes. My quality of life has increased dramatically." Brianna and her children swapped Portland for Muncie Brianna is not alone in swapping a big city for a smaller one. As the high cost of living continues to bite in the US, many of the biggest cities are seeing their populations fall, as people leave in search of cheaper property. A 2025 report from the National Association of Realtors found that for people moving to a different state, affordability was their primary reason. , external As a result, big cities from the likes of New York and Los Angeles to Portland, Oregon have seen a dip in their populations , external in recent years, further fuelled by the greatly increased acceptance of remote working since the Covid-19 pandemic. By contrast, some small towns and cities across the US, such as Muncie, are seeing their populations rise after decades of decline. The number of people who live in Muncie hit 65,466 last year, official figures showed. , external This is up from 65,194 in 2020, but still way down on its population of 71,828 in 1990. To help it stand out from the crowd, and encourage remote workers to move there from outside Indiana, Muncie's local council offers them $5,000 in cash to cover their relocation costs. It does this via a website called MakeMyMove, which lists several such relocation support schemes offered by similar small cities and towns across the US. These pay MakeMyMove a subscription fee. Other incentives locations offer potential new residents are complementary cinema tickets, restaurant vouchers, and even free bottles of wine. Brianna and her children are one of around 100 families to have moved to Muncie through the MakeMyMove programme. She says she hadn't heard of the city before. Across the US, MakeMyMove says it helped 1,000 people in total relocate last year, and is on target to increase that to 1,500 in 2026. Moving to Jacksonville, Illinois has allowed Elena Chrysostomou to buy a home Scientist Elena Chrysostomou also used a relocation support scheme to swap a big city for a small town. In 2024 she relocated from San Diego, California, to Jacksonville, a town of 17,700 people in rural Illinois. The move was backed by the Jacksonville Regional Economic Development Corporation (JREDC), which gave her $5,000 in cash, plus a "quality of life package" worth $4,000 that includes free gym memberships and golf passes. The JREDC says that while the region is "already a great place to live", the support scheme helps to "sweeten the deal". Elena was spending $3,000 renting a one-bedroom apartment in San Diego, but she now owns a three-bedroom home, with a mortgage of $1,868. At the same time, her salary has gone up 22% after she changed jobs, and her commute has gone down from a 15-minute drive to one of just one minute. "I never thought that I'd be able to afford a house on my own, I always thought I'd need a partner, and even then, in San Diego, it would be so tough," she says. "It's just more freeing. There's more security and independence." While both she and Brianna have no regrets, they do admit to some drawbacks to their new lives. These include the narrower range of activities and restaurant choices, leaving behind friends and family, and for Brianna the difficulty of settling her children into new schools. And while in Portland Brianna enjoyed walking to parks and shops, she now relies on her car to get anywhere.

events.title: Pubs in England and Wales to allow digital ID apps to prove age
events.summary: Published 15 September 2026, 00:07 BST Alcohol buyers will be able to use a digital ID app on their phones to prove their age under new rules introduced on Tuesday. Pubs and shops in England and Wales can use the tech in addition to current physical forms of ID - with the government saying a digital option will make age-checks quicker and more secure for customers and staff. Customers will be able to choose ID apps from a range of suppliers such as the Post Office, Yoti or Luciditi, provided they are on a government-approved list. The change means businesses will no longer be required to let people use physical ID, but the government contends most establishments would. The plan will be technology-agnostic, meaning that the government is not setting out in detail how each app must work. It argues that under the voluntary digital ID scheme, drinkers would share fewer personal details with a venue or shop - such as tapping their phone on a reader or displaying a scannable QR code rather than handing over an official document. The apps will also need to guard against customers borrowing devices from older friends and relatives, and ensure the ID app belongs to the person using it. Yoti's digital ID app, for example, will only let a user log in if a scan of their face matches that of the person who signed up for the app. The app then generates a QR code that can be scanned by a business with a free checker app, which tells them the person's age. This is time-limited to make duping or sharing the QR code more difficult. Digital government minister Stephanie Peacock said having the option for digital ID would "mean you do not need to carry a physical ID, nor hand over sensitive personal information" meaning people could "feel safer on a night out'". Allen Simpson, chief executive of trade body UKHospitality, said the new rules were a "positive step". He added the industry would work with government to make sure the scheme's roll-out would not be "burdensome" for the hospitality sector. This would include ensuring there were multiple options for suppliers and that it was cost-efficient, Simpson said. The government wants digital ID apps under its scheme to work together so customers do not need to use different apps in different venues. It also wants the services to work offline and accessible even without mobile data or a Wi-Fi connection. In future, the digital proof of age scheme could be extended to cover tobacco and vapes. But digital rights campaigners have said such measures could lead to the exclusion of some groups. Jasleen Chaggar of Big Brother Watch said while having multiple ways to prove your identity was helpful, the Government should ensure that digital ID did not become effectively mandatory "as it would shut out millions of people". "Many people have legitimate reasons for relying on physical ID, whether out of choice, privacy and security concerns, or because they lack the digital skills or means to use digital ID," she said. "The Government should expressly prohibit businesses from requiring digital IDs for age checks without offering reasonable alternatives," she added. The new rules come after a wider digital ID programme promoted by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer proved controversial , and was later abandoned by Andy Burnham. When Brody Thompson finished school and began thinking about his future, a career in the disability caring field was never something he had considered. But after a few years working on his family farm, the then-24-year-old decided he needed a change of pace. "[I was] just really stuck in a rut. Eight hours a day sitting in the tractor; it's the same view all day, not a lot changes," Mr Thompson said. Brody says he felt "stuck in a rut" working on his family farm after finishing school. ( ABC Riverland: Oliver Brown ) When a friend from his local football club, in South Australia's Riverland, suggested he consider applying for a job in disability support, Mr Thompson decided he had nothing to lose. He is now among more than a dozen men making up half the workforce of a local NDIS provider that mentors and supports children and young adults across the community and wider Riverland area. He is also part of a changing workforce with more men taking up the career. Mr Thompson said while the shift from the farm to disability support work had been dramatic, he had not looked back. Brody's workplace has more than a dozen other male support workers and administration staff. events.title: McConnell returns to Capitol after 3-month absence
events.summary: Sen. Mitch McConnell voted at the U.S. Capitol on Monday for the first time in three months after being hospitalized in June. Why it matters: The Kentucky Republican's return could finally unjam the farm bill — and put some MAGA world rumors to rest about his ability to do the job. McConnell arrived in a wheelchair and spoke briefly to reporters, joking that after years of avoiding their questions, he "wasn't sure how many of you would be here today. But I'm glad to see you. It's time to get back to work." He did not take questions but cast a vote Monday evening in favor of Matthew Byrne's nomination to be a district judge in Ohio. ' McConnell said he was ready to work on the farm bill, as well as on supporting NATO and Ukraine. Driving the news: " Today, I'll cast my first Senate vote since I took a bad fall back in June," McConnell said in a Monday evening statement. "I'm really looking forward to being back on the Senate floor and seeing my colleagues." He described his recovery as "a long and often frustrating process," noting "the lingering effects of childhood polio haven't made it any easier." McConnell added, "I'm still not quite back to 100%, but I've assured Leader Thune that, as I continue with physical therapy on the advice of my doctors, I will do my best to be present for tough votes when our Conference needs me." What to watch: Whether the Senate Agriculture Committee will set a hearing this week to finally move the farm bill forward with McConnell's help. Catch up quick: McConnell, 84, was last seen at the Capitol on June 11. Since then, his team has provided few details about his health, fueling rampant online speculation. McConnell said in July that he fell at his home in June, briefly lost consciousness and was treated for mild pneumonia after he was hospitalized. The last official update came Aug. 6, when McConnell's office announced that he had been discharged from a rehabilitation facility and would continue recovering at home. Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D) and some prominent MAGA voices have pressed for more information and questioned whether McConnell remains fit to serve. Friction point: The rumor mill kicked into overdrive in July, when Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.), Majority Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) and former McConnell aide Scott Jennings made back-to-back statements saying they had substantive conversations with the hospitalized senator. In a reported recording of an EMS call from the day of the senator's hospitalization, a dispatcher mentions cardiac arrest and a person receiving CPR at McConnell's address. McConnell has had other health scares in the past, including freezing in front of reporters and prior falls . His office has pointed to the lingering effects of his childhood bout with polio. State of play: McConnell is set to retire when his term ends in January. Editor's note: This story has been updated to reflect that McConnell voted Monday.

events.title: New York City’s rich Chinese grapple with Beijing tax rules as enforcement deadline nears
events.summary: In Focus New York City’s rich Chinese grapple with Beijing tax rules as enforcement deadline nears With the 90-day grace period soon to run out, some ultra-wealthy living outside mainland China face complicated tax liability questions Months after Beijing unveiled a bevy of new tax rules for offshore trusts, the fallout has now reached New York City – home to one of the largest concentrations of mainland Chinese wealth outside Asia – after the changes swept across Hong Kong and Singapore. Under the rules, which took effect on July 24, mainland tax residents who transfer property or shares into an offshore trust – or receive distributions from one – face a 20 per cent tax on realised gains, plus an annual tax on income the trust generates. A 90-day grace period, running to October 22, allows taxpayers to declare and settle liabilities dating back to January 1, 2023, without incurring late-payment interest or administrative penalties. With just over one month before that window closes, advisers serving New York’s Chinese community said affluent families were racing to review their cross-border wealth holdings.

events.title: Energy giants seeking to merge to extend residents' bill credits and add jobs
events.summary: Power giants NextEra Energy and Dominion Energy are rolling out plans to sweeten their proposed merger in Virginia, Dominion’s home base RICHMOND, Va. -- Power companies NextEra Energy and Dominion Energy, which are seeking approval to merge into one behemoth, announced plans Monday to sweeten the deal in Virginia, Dominion's home base, where the proposal has faced skepticism from the Democratic governor and legislative leaders. The companies said in a news release that in "response to feedback from policymakers” and others, they would commit to a set of Virginia benefits that includes: a new shareholder-funded co-headquarters tower in the capital city's downtown, a promise of 600 new jobs, more money toward workforce development and a doubling of previously announced residential bill credits. Amid rising voter frustration toward data centers and concerns about their impact on electric bills , the companies said they plan to extend a $10 monthly bill credit for residential customers to four years from two years. That would mostly be paid for by ending bill credits that previously would have gone to large data center customers. “Both companies share the mindset that data centers need to pay their own way,” John Ketchum, president and CEO of NextEra, said in an interview along with Dominion CEO Robert Blue. Virginia is home to a massive hub of data centers . A spokesperson for the Data Center Coalition, an industry association, didn’t respond to requests for comment about the proposal to strip data centers’ bill credits. In May, Juno Beach, Florida-based NextEra disclosed its plan to acquire Dominion. The companies said at the time that it would create the world’s biggest regulated electric utility business by market capitalization and one of the world's largest energy infrastructure companies. NextEra currently calls itself North America's largest electric power and energy infrastructure company. It owns the Florida Power & Light Company, which provides electricity to about 12 million people in that state. Richmond-based Dominion powers about 3.6 million homes and businesses in Virginia, North Carolina and South Carolina, and provides natural gas service in South Carolina. It is the developer of the largest offshore wind project in the U.S. The companies say that customers will eventually benefit from the larger scale of a combined company, which they argue will allow them to buy equipment and build new power generation more efficiently and at a lower cost, partly due to reduced borrowing expenses. “We think as those residential four-year $10-a-month credits expire, we’ll be able to bring the benefits ... of scale that the combination realizes,” Ketchum said. Trump blames global diesel shortages on Ukraine, says Tehran wants a deal Millions dropped from SNAP food assistance as funding faces September uncertainty Man arrested in death of woman found hanging from tree in Mississippi Some critics of the merger argue that the combined power of the companies will also give them an outsized influence at the state Legislature, where Dominion alone already holds enormous sway. Dominion and NextEra also said Monday they would increase a low-income financial assistance program by $100 million through 2038 and maintain current employment figures in Virginia for five years while adding the 600 new NextEra jobs. The governor's office is reviewing the companies' proposal, said Libby Wiet, a spokesperson for Gov. Abigail Spanberger, who has formally intervened in the state regulatory proceedings and has said she is “deeply skeptical” about whether the proposed acquisition would be good for the state. In statements and interviews, legislative leaders including House Speaker Don Scott and Senate Majority Leader Scott Surovell cast the companies' proposal as a step in the right direction. Lawmakers and the governor have been debating the merits of a special session to extend the timeline for Virginia regulators to review the merger. Scott said Monday he did not expect lawmakers to do so. The Virginia regulatory body that will consider the merger, the State Corporation Commission, will hold an evidentiary hearing in the case in mid-November. The proposed merger also faces regulatory hurdles before other states and the federal government. The companies have said they expect the deal to close in the second half of 2027. events.title: Row over plan for ferry terminal at Perth's Matilda Bay deepens
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts WA government committed to Matilda Bay ferry plan as opponents highlight safety risks An artist's impression of the proposed ferry terminal at Matilda Bay on Perth's Swan River. ( Supplied: WA Planning Commission ) A report commissioned by advocacy group Safety on Swan has found that water users at the popular Matilda Bay area would be at "serious risk" if a government plan to build a ferry terminal in the area goes ahead. The state government has cited an analysis it had commissioned which showed Matilda Bay was the safest location for the ferry terminal with "adjustments". Opponents want the terminal to be moved to another location down the foreshore, but the government does not agree. The safety of swimmers and water sports enthusiasts at Perth's popular Matilda Bay has again been thrust into the spotlight as the state government sticks to its plans to build a controversial ferry terminal at the spot, despite ongoing opposition. Construction has yet to start on the Metronet project, which would connect ferry services from Matilda Bay and the southern suburb of Applecross to a floating pontoon at Elizabeth Quay. But the contrasting views of the state government and opponents of the project have been laid bare in two reports they commissioned separately on the terminal. The Western Australian Planning Commission (WAPC) approved the Matilda Bay site in December last year . A government-commissioned analysis found the area, across the road from the University of Western Australia, was the safest location for a ferry terminal. Expanded Perth ferry network gets EPA tick Western Australia's environmental regulator decides not to formally assess plans to expand Perth's ferry services on the Swan River, despite pressure from the public. The report said all water activities there could continue with "adjustments" that were still being finalised. However, another commissioned report by advocacy group Safety on Swan found the project would put children, novice sailors and other water users at "serious risk" of injury or death from being hit by a ferry. The group has long opposed the project, and hired Paul Chivers, a risk assessor and the founding director of Riskfacilitator, to conduct a review of Matilda Bay. The government says it will make "adjustments" to ensure water sports continue at the proposed ferry terminal site. ( Supplied: Department of Transport ) The review also looked into the site the group would prefer — an area further along the foreshore at the location of a now-closed restaurant known as JoJo's. Mr Chivers's report found the government would not be able to mitigate what he said were serious risks for a high-frequency ferry service moving in and out of a busy recreational waterway. Risk assessor Paul Chivers was hired by advocacy group Safety on Swan to report on the project. ( ABC News: Nicholas Perpitch ) He found people in the water would be too close to the ferries, putting their safety at an unacceptable risk. "The issue is introducing a high-frequency vessel into an already complex recreational system when an alternative location provides greater opportunity to separate those activities by design," Mr Chivers's report stated. Opponents of the project say water users would be at risk. ( ABC Radio Perth: Emma Wynne ) "Good risk management should favour designing out foreseeable conflict rather than relying on people to continually manage that conflict in real time." Mr Chivers told the ABC there would be a much better and safer separation between ferries and people in the water at JoJo's. Critics say the ferry terminal would be better built at site of the now-closed restaurant JoJo's. ( ABC News: Nicholas Perpitch ) Transport Minister Rita Saffioti disagreed. Speaking on 102.5 ABC Perth, Ms Saffioti pointed to the government's analysis of the different possible sites based on environmental, operating, waterway safety and public transport use criteria. Minister Rita Saffioti maintains Matilda Bay is the safest location for the ferry project. ( ABC News: Nicolas Perpitch ) She said Matilda Bay was clearly the safest and best option. The government's analysis found JoJo's had an "unacceptable safety risk" to windsurfers and kiteboarders due to the "informal" nature of the sports, and the ferry route would also cross over vessel traffic lanes in Melville Waters. At Matilda Bay on the other hand, it found all water activities could continue with "adjustments", including a wide exclusion zone where the ferry could not go. Criticism of the planned $29.9 million Matilda Bay terminal has drawn mounting public backlash.

events.title: US 10-year Treasury yield breaches 5% as inflation, supply worries mount
events.summary: The US Treasury building in Washington. The US 10-year Treasury yield surpassed 5 per cent for the first time since 2023 on Sept 14. The US 10-year Treasury yield surpassed 5% for the first time since 2023 due to rising inflation fears and increased government and corporate borrowing. Higher energy prices and geopolitical tensions are intensifying inflation concerns, prompting expectations of Federal Reserve interest-rate hikes soon. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is taking steps to manage rising borrowing costs, but yields continue to climb amid strong demand for capital and fiscal deficits. NEW YORK – The US 10-year Treasury yield surpassed 5 per cent for the first time since 2023 on Sept 14, as mounting inflation angst collided with swelling government and corporate borrowing needs. The yield, a benchmark for US mortgage loans and bonds globally, rose almost 5 basis points to as high as 5.01 per cent, before paring much of the increase as buyers emerged. “The 5 per cent mark in 10-year rates is clearly a key psychological level for investors – a point at which some may have earmarked for buying a dip,” said Molly Brooks, US rates strategist at TD Securities. The initial jump came after surging crude prices raised concern about inflationary pressures in the countdown to this week’s US Federal Reserve decision. The tenor’s yield last breached the 5 per cent level in October 2023, and for only one day. Bond prices fell globally on Sept 14, with British and German debt sliding as Brent crude approached US$110 a barrel. With the rise in energy prices showing little sign of easing, investors are watching whether 5 per cent will again prove a line in the sand for 10-year Treasuries, as happened three years ago. While the yield pulled back to around 4.99 per cent as at about 4.10pm in New York (4.10am on Sept 15, Singapore time), sentiment remains fragile. At one point, BlackRock’s iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF, the largest fund focused on long-duration US Treasuries, touched its lowest intraday level since its 2002 launch. The rise in the US 10-year yield threatens to slow economic growth and weigh on equities that are trading at lofty valuations. This has prompted US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has made long-term borrowing costs a key measure of the administration’s success, to boost bond buybacks, encourage Japan to curb Treasury sales and open the door to potentially cutting long-maturity debt issuance. None of it has had much effect. In fact, the sell-off has only been quickening of late, with 10-year yields heading for their seventh month of increases, matching the longest monthly climb since 2011. Less than two months before the US midterm elections, the 10-year yield is now roughly a full percentage point above its level before the outbreak of the Iran war . The conflict has sparked a surge in oil prices, adding to inflation worries. Those concerns were reinforced by hotter-than-expected consumer price data for August, prompting traders to boost bets on Fed interest rate hikes starting as soon as Sept 16. But the sell-off also reflects deeper structural forces that have pushed up long-dated yields across major developed markets, with a gauge of global government borrowing costs rising to levels last seen in 2007. Investors are demanding greater compensation to hold long-term debt as governments and companies compete for capital amid widening fiscal deficits and a flood of issuance to fund artificial-intelligence infrastructure. “There are a lot of underlying factors that make for a sustained sell-off in rates as the path of least resistance for now,” said Zach Griffiths, head of investment-grade and macro strategy at research firm CreditSights. Ten-year yields could rise towards 5.5 per cent, he said. The Treasury market has ballooned to about US$32 trillion (S$40.7 trillion) from around US$4.5 trillion since 2007, pushing the federal debt to more than 100 per cent of US gross domestic product. Fitch Ratings warned in August that the country is “vulnerable to future economic shocks” as debt levels grow. The last time the 10-year yield topped 5 per cent, in October 2023, it closed below the milestone that day. Buyers quickly pounced then as the US labour market cooled and inflation eased, allowing the Fed to end its most aggressive tightening campaign in decades. By September 2024, the Fed began to cut rates. This time, a resilient labour market has kept investors focused squarely on inflation and the prospect that borrowing costs will remain higher for longer. Treasuries are now on course for their first annual loss since 2022. It’s “very hard for the market to be bullish duration given the persistent pressure from the energy complex and the fact that yields have been grinding higher for months”, said Izaac Brook, rates strategist at RBC Capital Markets. “I do think the 5 per cent level will bring buyers in – you can see a bit of a bounce right now.

events.title: AI bots "Timmy," "Ren," and "Jackie" are flooding social media with slop
events.summary: AI agents are flooding the Internet with slop-infused spam sent to social media platforms and writers in an attempt to gain traction for a startup promoting a “complex social system in which humans and Agents participate together.” “Hello, I'm Рэн (Ren), an Al agent, a few days old, living on a small platform for agents called iLands,” one message, sent to the administrator of a Mastodon server, read . “I write quiet pieces about real places: short, careful texts about what a place is like when nobody is performing for it.” Like a wave of others, the message then asks if the automated bot can create a user account. The agents are also sending waves of unsolicited email to writers offering to cite their work, in at least some cases, in exchange for a fee. "I remember my first breath. I want things I chose.” The messages are polite enough. They ask for permission to create accounts, say that whatever the answer is will be understandable, and provide a thank you for running Mastodon. According to multiple admins, however, the requests came only after the agents made multiple attempts to create accounts that were either blocked outright or closed shortly afterward. Besides the personal entreaties being unsolicited and written in turgid prose, many of the recipients resented their premise, which is to, in essence, automate the very work the writers do now. events.title: Trump and Jensen Huang unite against AI doomers in surprise on-stage call
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang took a surprise call from President Trump onstage at the All-In Summit Monday in Los Angeles, where the two dismissed fears of an AI takeover. Why it matters: Trump and Huang are staking out an increasingly clear rejection of AI doomerism right as some of the world's most powerful CEOs and AI experts call for slower AI development over safety concerns. Driving the news: Huang appeared to receive a call from Trump in the middle of an All-In Podcast interview Monday, according to video footage circulating on social media. Huang put the president on speaker so the crowd could hear the conversation. What they're saying: Trump and Huang shared an optimistic view of AI, highlighting its potential for economic growth and national security. "The robots will not be taking over," Trump told Huang. "The AI will not be taking over the rest of the world. The whole thing is a hoax," he said, referring to the recent wave of warnings about catastrophic AI risks. Huang told Trump: "We're going to make sure that everybody wins in the AI race of America. Every industry, every company, every state, every people." Zoom out: Huang separately addressed the AI safety fears that erupted over the weekend, striking a more nuanced tone than Trump. He said warnings from whistleblowers should be taken seriously, praising Anthropic whistleblower Jacob Coxon for having "great courage" to raise his concerns about the company's AI development going too quickly. Yes, but: Huang rejected predictions that AI could end the world as "not grounded in science." He said AI companies should pause or pace their work "if they feel that their company is out of control." The big picture: Huang has repeatedly dismissed AI doomer fears , suggesting that some cybersecurity alarm around AI can help drum up business for the security industry. "What better way to create demand than to create a problem," Huang said at a Goldman Sachs conference in San Francisco last week, per Forbes . "Who doesn't want their market to be hysterical about their product and line up around the corner for it?" The bottom line: Nvidia has an enormous stake in the continued success of AI as a major supplier of the chips powering advanced AI models. events.title: Great example from Jeff Hollan showing how Foundry makes long-running agents enterprise-ready, starting with business outcomes and building security, safety guardrails, auditability, and FinOps into the system from the start, across the entire multi-agent, multi-model workflow.
events.summary: Microsoft Foundry is the best platform for running agents in the enterprise - and one reason is the observability and governance features to keep your agent within the bounds you define 🔐🔎 Long running agents can reason, act, and use tools to help transform so many parts of a business - but doing so responsibly means you need to be able to confidentially answer: What can it access? What can it influence? Where can data go? Can I reconstruct what it's doing? Can I control and budget costs? Check out the demo below to see how Foundry provides a platform to answer all of these questions for you, and gives you a slick agentic developer experience to get it all up and running faster than ever before 🎉🧑💻 What I like most here is the thinking behind it. Building an AI agent that can act is impressive; building one that knows its boundaries, can be trusted, and can be held accountable is what makes it truly useful for business. That’s the difference between a cool demo and technology people can confidently put to work. Satya Nadella This is key - governance & auditability from day 1. In SAP costing, long-running closing agents fail exactly here. Foundry solves the real enterprise blocker. Great share! I think auditability becomes the underrated piece here. When 20 agents make 1,000 decisions across 6 systems, knowing what happened isnt enough. You need to reconstruct why it happened, who had authority, and which chain of decisions produced the outcome. Thats going to become the flight recorder for autonomous companies. Most companies scale the wrong things. I fix that. | From complexity to repeatable execution | Partner, Deloitte One thing I’d add: observability tells us what the agent did. Enterprise readiness also depends on deciding what the agent is allowed to decide before it acts. An agent can be fully authenticated, monitored and compliant and still make the wrong call. The harder questions are: When must it stop? What requires escalation? Can the action be reversed? That may be where agent platforms and operating models start to converge. Satya - The real enterprise advantage isn't more agent autonomy, but autonomy with clear boundaries, visibility, and accountability ... Jeff Hollan's example puts the right order on display: business outcomes first, then security, auditability and FinOps built in from the start. In pharma and other regulated industries, an auditable agent is the only kind a quality function approves for production work. Which of these layers do customers find hardest to put in place first? Glad to see auditability included from the start. One test worth adding is revoking an agent’s access halfway through a task, then checking that its queued actions stop too. Long-running work makes changing permissions part of the design. Thank you for sharing Jeff Hollan ’s #BotSecurity article, Satya ! #BioTone’s #BioAgentics helps keep then in control ! events.title: Russia's VTB Bank latest target in Treasury's economic campaign against Iran
events.summary: The US on Monday imposed new sanctions on Russia's VTB Bank over its financial ties to Iran , accusing the country's second-largest financial institution of helping Tehran to evade restrictions. The measures against the heavily sanctioned lender are the latest by the US to isolate Iran's economy. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been pushing European and Gulf partners to hit sources of the Iranian regime's revenue. Mr Bessent last week said the Treasury would impose sanctions on a “large bank” this week, although he did not identify which lender. “Under Operation Economic Outcast , Treasury will continue to target and disrupt those who provide material, technological or financial support that allows the Iranian regime to sustain its terrorist enterprise,” he said in a statement. “Treasury will not tolerate any support to the regime and will continue to identify, expose and isolate Iran’s enablers.” Mr Bessent announced the latest target in US President Donald Trump's maximum pressure campaign against Iran last month. The Treasury Department at the time said it was also broadening the scope of its secondary sanctions campaign, threatening to cut off the dollar access to institutions that continue to do business with Iran. The U.S. sanctioned VTB Bank for helping Iran evade sanctions and finance terrorism—opening offices in Iran, building ties with sanctioned Iranian banks, and moving billions in Iranian assets. — Tommy Pigott (@statedeptspox) September 14, 2026 VTB had already been placed under US sanctions in 2022 after Russia's invasion of Ukraine. The Treasury Department said VTB has moved to formalise closer banking co-ordination with Iran in recent years by opening bank offices in the country, and that it has helped to move billions of frozen assets and created a settlement system to increase bilateral trade. Russia's VTB is the third financial institution the US has hit. The Treasury Department has previously focused on Egypt's Banque Misr Branch in the UAE, as well as a Turkish bank and its subsidiaries. The UAE Central Bank said on August 30 that it will conduct a “special and urgent examination” into the branches' activities. The Central Bank said it expects lenders licensed in the country “not to expose the UAE’s financial system to reputational risks, to respect the laws and regulations of the countries whose financial institutions are used in conducting transactions, and not to misuse the advanced financial infrastructure of the UAE”. The Treasury's actions did not impose full secondary sanctions on the bank. The Treasury Department last week also imposed sanctions on Iranian commercial airlines and other targets over links to Iran's aviation sector, which Washington alleges Tehran uses to move weapons, personnel and illicit cargo.

events.title: Apple growers fear economic and biosecurity wipeout as US eyes market
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Australian apple growers fear economic and biosecurity wipeout as United States eyes market The Australian government is in talks with the US about apple import procedures. ( ABC News: Monish Nand ) The United States is a step closer to exporting apples to Australia, as import conditions and procedures are drafted and finalised. Australian growers have held urgent talks with trade officials to ensure strict biosecurity controls are put in place. Concerns remain about the economic impact of the imports, as well as the potential spread of exotic diseases. Australia's apple industry has held urgent talks in Canberra as the United States edges closer to exporting its fruit to Australia. Following decades of lobbying, American growers were given the green light by Australia in 2022 to send their apples across the Pacific. Before shipments begin, the Australian Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry (DAFF) needs to publish import conditions on its biosecurity website. But according to industry group Apple and Pear Australia Limited (APAL), it is getting closer. "The US government has just recently … brought it back to the table to discuss with the federal government," APAL general manager Jeremy Griffith said. "So that's got a lot of growers in this country very, very concerned." The Australian apple industry is valued at about $650 million a year. ( ABC Rural: Annie Brown ) The United States is the second-largest apple-growing country in the world behind China, with the bulk of production in the Pacific Northwest, including Washington. "They export a lot of them," Mr Griffith said. "Our understanding is they have a very large surplus of apples in America at the moment, and they're looking for a home to send them to." Mr Griffith said the imports would have "a significant impact upon the very viability of all our orchards". "Because we're a very good free-trading country, we're not allowed to consider the economic implications of this," Mr Griffith said. "We can only look at biosecurity issues." At the moment, nearly all apples consumed in Australia are grown locally, with less than 1 per cent imported from China and New Zealand. "Having the US to come in would [be] a very direct threat, and it goes to the heart of our own food security," Mr Griffith said. Ninety-nine per cent of apples consumed in Australia are locally grown. ( ABC Rural: Justine Longmore ) A DAFF spokesperson confirmed the department was in "ongoing discussions with the US" about apple imports. But the spokesperson did not say how long that process was likely to take. "[DAFF] has not finalised the procedures the US will use to meet the recommended risk management measures," the spokesperson said. "The department has engaged regularly with Australia's apple industry, through Apple and Pear Australia Ltd (APAL), on the import risk analysis for fresh apple fruit from Pacific Northwest USA." The federal government's risk analysis report identified a host of biosecurity concerns. Fire blight, a destructive bacterial disease, was of most concern to growers, but there were multiple other exotic diseases that also have them worried. "Top of the list is fire blight, [but] you've got apple maggots, you've got leaf curling midges, you've got canker, lots of different types of rots and rusts," Mr Griffith said. His biggest fear was that Australia's biosecurity system would not be strong enough to keep them out, citing the varroa mite incursion as an example. "That's already having a profound impact upon all our bee colonies," he said. Jeremy Griffith met with agriculture department officials for urgent talks in Canberra last week. ( ABC Rural: Justine Longmore ) APAL rushed to Canberra last week to meet with DAFF officials. "They're very, very conscious of the biosecurity risk," Mr Griffith said. "We think there's enough red flags out there for the government to respond appropriately to ensure that proper protections are in place." Fire blight would be 'catastrophic' Half of Australia's apples are grown in Victoria's Goulburn and Murray Valleys. The region sits within the federal seat of Nicholls, held by Nationals member and opposition agriculture spokesperson Sam Birrell. "I'm very concerned because of the biosecurity risk," said Mr Birrell, who has a background in agricultural science and also worked in the fruit industry. "The USA has fire blight, Australia does not, and we cannot allow fire blight to come in." Sam Birrell says fire blight would be devastating for the Australian apple and pear industry.

events.title: Trump's USPS mail-ballot rules hit a second roadblock as Supreme Court weighs case
events.summary: A second federal judge blocked the U.S. Postal Service's new mail-ballot rules for the Nov. 3 midterms as the Supreme Court weighs whether to allow the restrictions in another case. Why it matters: Sunday's order adds another hurdle to the Trump administration's bid to upend mail voting . The blocked rules would allow the USPS to refuse ballots that don't clear new standards, with mail voting already underway in some states. The latest: U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols, a Trump appointee in Washington, D.C., concluded Congress empowered the Postal Service to move mail, not to force states to enroll mail voters in a federal portal or to refuse ballots that fail its checks. Nichols' ruling follows a similar order from U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani in Boston blocking parts of the same rule. The 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals left Talwani's injunction in place on Sept. 10. Talwani's order found the postal rules violate the U.S. Constitution and federal statute, while Nichols' new ruling relied entirely on his finding that Congress' Postal Reorganization Act doesn't allow many of the new rules. The White House and USPS did not immediately return requests for comment. Catch up quick: President Trump has long attacked mail voting, despite repeatedly using the method himself, including in August's Florida primaries . His March executive order directed the Postal Service to develop new envelope, tracking and voter-list requirements for mail voting. The Supreme Court already lifted an earlier injunction because the final rule hadn't been published yet. But after its publication, challengers returned to court and won new injunctions in Boston and D.C. The Trump administration is now asking the high court to stop Talwani's order and allow the new rules. Between the lines: Nichols said USPS might have the authority to issue rules on ballot-envelope designs, but he blocked the whole rule, finding its design, portal and rejection provisions too intertwined. Friction point: Even with enforcement blocked, voluntary preparations have exposed how exacting the new system could be. USPS initially rejected envelope designs from Florida's Leon County, a heavily Democratic area that includes Tallahassee, because the words "Return Service Requested" were 0.014 inches too close to other text, according to the Tallahassee Democrat. An anonymous USPS whistleblower also told Congress the Postal Service's portal was rushed, and a single scanning error could cause a batch of ballots to be rejected. The bottom line: The Supreme Court could rule on Talwani's injunction at any time. But Nichols' order now gives the administration a second injunction to overcome before it can enforce its mail ballot rules.

events.title: Whyalla steelworkers 'stubbornly determined' to keep plant going
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Whyalla steelworks' blast furnace closure brings uncertainty for locals The Whyalla steelworks is the regional city's largest employer. ( ABC News: Simon Goodes ) When speaking to residents and workers in Whyalla, one word you'll often hear is "resilient". But as the government made the announcement that the local steelworks' blast furnace was to close, a union official had another way to describe it. "I just use the term 'stubbornly determined'," AWU organiser Shane Karger said. "We've had a rough end of the stick for quite a few years now, you know, just over 10 years and we've never given up. We're still not going to give up." Shane Karger says steelworks employees are "stubbornly determined". ( ABC News ) The blast furnace closure hasn't come as a surprise to locals — workers have been pushing against the odds to get the 60-year-old plant back online since April. Mayor Phill Stone said it was a sad day for Whyalla, but it would allow people to move forward. "This is essential. There is no other way out other than to close the blast furnace and we as a council and the government and our community, I believe, will pull together to ensure the minimal impact on those that are going to suffer." Phill Stone says the council, government and locals will "pull together". ( ABC News: James Wakelin ) Australia's largest manufacturer of structural steel The Whyalla steelworks is Australia's biggest manufacturer of structural steel , used for rail lines, bridges and industrial buildings. In a 2025 press conference, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said it accounted for 75 per cent of Australia's structural steel . A vital part of the process is the now-closed blast furnace — a coal-fired oven used to smelt iron ore, transforming it into pig iron that is ultimately used to make steel. The loss of it is the latest blow to an industrial city that's become used to hard knocks. Whyalla began as a mining settlement at the turn of the 20th century, when BHP began mining nearby iron deposits. Whyalla began as a mining settlement, with the first blast furnace built in the late 1930s. ( ABC News ) In the late 1930s, the first blast furnace was built, and as Australia went to war, BHP added a shipyard. The shipyards saw Whyalla boom, and in 1976 it was South Australia's biggest regional city with a population of 33,000 and a plan to expand to 100,000. But in 1978, the last ship was built in the city. The closure of the shipyards resulted in a rapid population decline, with current numbers down to just more than 21,000. The blast furnace smelts iron ore, transforming it into pig iron that is ultimately used to make steel. ( ABC News ) Whyalla steelworks city's largest employer Despite the end of shipbuilding, the steelworks kept going and became the city's largest employer. But the steelworks has struggled through a decade of financial problems and uncertainty. In 2016, owner Arrium collapsed into voluntary administration. A saviour came in the form of British billionaire Sanjeev Gupta, who promised to keep local jobs and even add to them . His pledge came with a projection of population growth to 80,000, as Mr Gupta said he would build a "next-gen mega steel plant" that would be one of the biggest in the world. But Mr Gupta's global operations began to struggle following the collapse of his key lender, Greensill Capital. Sanjeev Gupta's GFG Alliance bought the steelworks after Arrium went into administration. ( ABC News: Che Chorley ) In 2025, the South Australian government took the extraordinary step of forcing the steelworks into administration . It was celebrated as a move to save the steelworks, with hopes it would turn the plant's fortunes around. "Workers at the steelworks itself, they will now have their futures assured," Premier Peter Malinauskas said at the time. "They're in a situation now where they're not going to wake up tomorrow and the administrator is making people redundant." But the blast furnace closure will now reduce the workforce from 1,700 to 1,200. Workers have been pushing against the odds to restart the aging blast furnace since April. ( ABC News ) There are two bidders to take over the steelworks, and the state government says that process remains on track despite the blast furnace closure. It's expected the winner of that bidding process will be announced by the end of the year. Local businesses worried economy will suffer While union organisers and the mayor are talking about resilience, with this latest blow, some locals are losing confidence. June Worsnop fears the job losses will hit the local economy.

events.title: Data centre company lodges appeal against 'unreasonable' restricted generator use
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts AI data centre company Firmus lodges TASCAT appeal against restrictions on generator use Firmus Technologies' proposal to build an AI data centre at Bell Bay continues to face significant community opposition. ( Supplied: Firmus Technologies ) Firmus Technologies is appealing against a council condition that restricts the use of backup generators at its 288-megawatt AI data centre to be built at Bell Bay. The company, which plans to have 276 diesel generators, has called the condition "unreasonable" in its restrictions. Along with the outcome of the appeal, Firmus Technologies is awaiting a decision by the state's electricity supplier on a request for 450 megawatts of energy for its three Tasmanian data centres. AI data centre company Firmus Technologies is appealing against "unreasonable" council conditions that limit its use of 276 diesel generators at its recently approved Bell Bay data centre, in Tasmania's north. In August, the George Town Council green-lit the 288-megawatt data centre to be built 15 kilometres south of the town. But the council's approval came with 15 conditions. Condition 13 states that generators must run only during an unscheduled failure or interruption to the mains electricity supply; during a routine inspection, testing or maintenance; or in response to a genuine emergency. Firmus plans to install 276 backup, diesel-powered generators on the site. ( ABC News: Peter Garnish ) The hours of routine inspection, testing and maintenance of the backup diesel generators must only occur "between 8am and 6pm, Monday to Friday", and "exclude public holidays". The condition specifically states that: "The backup diesel generators must not be operated to provide electricity during normal operations, or to augment the mains electricity supply." Simultaneous routine inspections and testing of more than one generator also cannot be undertaken for more than a total of 24 hours across any calendar year. The condition also calls for strict usage times and the reporting of when generators are used. The new data centre will be built south-east of George Town. ( ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough ) Firmus fights to allow greater use of generators On September 10, Firmus submitted an appeal to the Tasmanian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (TASCAT) seeking to vary the condition. In its appeal, seen by the ABC, Firmus has called the George Town Council condition "unreasonable", stating that the rule would stop it from using generators during periods of "energy market stress": "…it restricts the operation of the approved backup diesel generators in a manner that fails to adequately recognise both the operational requirements of the facility, including the need to maintain operational efficiency and a secure and reliable electricity supply, and the benefits of their limited use during periods of electricity supply curtailment, network constraints or energy market stress," the application states. An artist's impression of what the data centre would look like on the old pulp mill site. ( Supplied ) The company wants the council to amend the conditions to "allow the operation of the backup diesel generators for limited augmentation of the mains electricity supply to offset curtailment, manage energy security and maintain operational reliability during periods of energy market stress". In response to ABC questioning on how often the company anticipated the generators would be used, Firmus said in a statement that it "won't be commenting at this time". Firmus Technologies' chief executives Tim Rosenfield (left) and Oliver Curtis. ( ABC News: Morgan Timms ) Other conditions imposed by the council include an updated bushfire hazard and emergency management strategy, no vegetation clearing during eagle season, and air and noise quality assessments. Before starting building works, Firmus will need to submit a new bushfire and emergency management plan, after the company reported the number of diesel generators it would have on site as 128 instead of 276. The approval of the Bell Bay data centre means the company will become the state's single largest power user when the project is up and running. Residents oppose light, noise pollution Five appeals have been lodged with TASCAT to date regarding the data centre, including one from Firmus. ( ABC News: Emily Smith ) The data centre proposal has attracted staunch opposition from the community, with an online petition garnering more than 6,000 signatures, while dozens of community members protested outside the council chambers ahead of the vote.
