events.title: Trump needs to listen to Africa to shape AGOA’s future
events.summary: At a moment when the US is reconsidering the extent and purpose of its engagement abroad, I find myself returning to a lesson I confronted often in my time in government: After more than five decades working on Africa, one of the most important things the US can do is show up and listen. The story of how the African Growth and Opportunity Act came together in 1999 is instructive as I recall in my memoir . We were preparing to roll out AGOA under the Clinton administration and invited the leadership of the African diplomatic corps to the State Department for a briefing. We told the ambassadors that only 10 countries would be selected and that their governments would be informed through our ambassadors in Africa. That went over like a lead balloon. The dean of the group, the highly respected Roble Olhaye of Djibouti, reminded us that the diplomatic corps had been advocating for AGOA for five years. They had been updating their capitals and lobbying Congress for the legislation. How, he asked, could we treat them in such a “shabby manner?” He was right. We had not been listening. So we changed course, inviting more than 180 ministers from 43 African countries to Washington for four days of discussions with President Bill Clinton, cabinet members, Congress, business leaders, and civil society representatives to discuss trade, investment, conflict prevention, food security, democracy, and human rights. We then went back to the list of potential AGOA beneficiaries and determined that 32 African countries met the conditions of the legislation. The rest, as they say, is history. More than a quarter-century later, AGOA is again in flux. Congress extended the program through the end of 2026, and the Trump administration has said it wants to modernize the legislation to align with its America First trade policy and create more opportunities for US businesses. This creates an opportunity to ask a bigger question: What should the US-Africa commercial relationship look like for the next 25 years? The answer should not be developed in Washington alone. Africa has changed dramatically since AGOA was created. It is building a continent-wide market, while its governments are seeking investment in manufacturing, energy, infrastructure, and technology, while looking to add value to their mineral resources. The US has interests of its own: new markets for American companies, resilient supply chains, and access to critical minerals. Those interests can align with African priorities, but Washington should not assume they do. That is why listening is a strategic tool, not simply a diplomatic courtesy. If Washington wants American companies to compete more effectively in Africa, it first needs to understand what its potential partners actually want. That is why the Trump administration should convene the US-Africa Ministerial called for in the recently extended AGOA legislation — and make the meeting more than a ceremonial gathering. It should bring together African governments, continent-wide blocs such as the African Union, US and African businesses, investors, and civil society to help shape the next generation of the relationship. The goal should be more than modernizing a trade preference program. It should be to identify where US and African interests genuinely intersect — and where they do not — and build policy around that reality. There is a broader lesson here for US policy toward Africa. A relationship centered more heavily on trade, investment, and mutually beneficial commercial opportunities can be entirely consistent with America’s interests. But transactional does not have to mean transactional-only. The most successful commercial relationships are built on knowledge, trust, and sustained engagement. My experience in 1999 taught me that showing up is not enough. You have to listen before you decide what the partnership should look like. That is as true for the next 25 years as it was for the first 25.

events.title: AI Leaders Are Calling for a Slowdown. Trump’s Team Says It’s on Them
events.summary: As calls for artificial intelligence regulation intensify, US President Donald Trump’s team have made it clear that if lab leaders want to implement an industry-wide slowdown , they’re going to have to do it themselves. Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei called on the US government to regulate AI companies within a wider effort to slow the pace of the technology’s development in an essay published Saturday. The essay received rare endorsement from both OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and Elon Musk, who owns chatbot Grok , following a week of intense debate about the technology’s threats to human safety. Microsoft chief executive officer Satya Nadella also called for pacing development. Calls for AI slowdown and regulation have intensified after a number of researchers voiced major concerns in the last week about the speed of the technology’s advance. “AI progress is increasing,” former DeepMind researcher Rishub Jain told WIRED . “And as AI becomes more capable, it poses more risks.” But David Sacks, co-chair of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, wrote on X, “If the unreleased models are scary enough that you think you should slow down, I support your decision to be responsible. But stop pretending you need anyone else’s permission. Stop pretending antitrust law has to be suspended so you can form a cartel … Most of all, stop pretending the motivation to slow down is purely altruistic.” Amodei had requested the government enable competing AI companies to work together on standards without breaching antitrust law, either by participating in discussions or issuing a waiver for the companies involved. He also called for government assistance in establishing international coordination, including with the Chinese Communist Party, though critics wondered how effective this would be. “China is very unlikely to join a global agreement, as you know,” Sacks wrote. Concerns about the US ceding its lead in the technology to China have caused the US government to mostly push back against the notion of slowing the pace of its development. “You have a lot of very negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn’t be bringing it up and they’re bringing up things that won’t happen,” Trump said during a visit to Ireland. “We’re leading China on AI,” he added, “and, frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins." The US largely views China’s AI ecosystem as an economic and national security threat and has previously been caught short by the country’s advances in the technology. “If Congress just races in and does some sort of emergency session to try to regulate AI, we will lose the race to China, and that is a threat to every single American,” House Speaker Mike Johnson told CNN on Sunday. “So, we’ve got to have balance. We’ve got to have steady hands at the wheel.” In the meantime, companies say they are going to start taking voluntary steps to reestablish public trust that they are acting responsibly. On Sunday night, OpenAI’s Altman committed to a proposal by Amodei to give embedded third-party evaluators employee-level access to their firms to check that practices and products are safe and to report incidents. While these measures will have “significant costs,” he wrote on X: “Pacing will be well worth this cost; no amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness.” In your inbox: WIRED's most ambitious, future-defining stories AI slop backlash is actually having an impact Big Story: The cop who took on Flock Watch: I stole a car by hacking this hidden device © 2026 Condé Nast. events.title: Uber paid drivers more than it charged passengers in Nigeria — report
events.summary: The News Uber was paying Nigerian drivers more than it charged passengers for some short trips, an unsustainable subsidy that played a leading role in the US ride-hailing giant’s abrupt exit this month , according to a new report based on thousands of Uber trips. The company quit Nigeria and Uganda on Sept. 2, the same day it announced a global restructuring decision that cut 10% of its staff globally . It still operates in four African countries including South Africa and Kenya. Even after 12 years of operating in Nigeria, Uber did not have a large enough number of active passengers there and high inflation and currency depreciation made passengers increasingly price sensitive, according to a report by Obi, a California-based price and trip data aggregator that tracks more than half-dozen ride hailing platforms. “It’s obvious that demand [in Nigeria] was low and that the political and economic climate wasn’t helping,” Ashwini Anburajan , CEO of Obi, told Semafor. “Pay had to be subsidized to make drivers willing to take rides. There was just no way for Uber to dig itself out of this pattern,” Anburajan said. Her firm’s data suggests that Uber paid Nigerian drivers more than it charged passengers on trips shorter than 12 miles (20 km). In some cases, the company paid drivers 23% more than the passenger was actually charged. Though the company adjusted this pattern above the 12-mile threshold, it amounted to an “over-generous” subsidy scheme for short rides that drivers would not have otherwise accepted, an approach that Uber’s in-country rivals like InDrive did not resort to, Obi said. A typical Uber driver in Nigeria averaged 130 rides over the first seven months of 2026, but that was just over a tenth of the volume of rides the company’s drivers in South Africa fulfilled over the same period, the report first shared with Semafor showed. Yet, Nigerian drivers kept a larger share of the fare paid by passengers compared to their counterparts in South Africa, the firm said. Its report is based on data from more than 20,000 rides completed by more than 300 drivers within the period on Uber and InDrive, a Russian-founded US company that also operates in Nigeria. Step Back Uber’s arrival in Nigeria in 2014 heralded a taxi revolution after a couple handful of startups attempted ride-hailing services in Lagos with little success. The company rode in aggressively with more than a billion dollars in investor capital to upstage the city’s often rickety yellow cabs, promising technology-aided transport efficiency to passengers and dependable income to drivers. This month’s decision to pull out came after several attempts to stay relevant, from floating courier services and boat taxis, to multiple fare rises implemented to reflect higher costs of doing business following economic policy changes that have been rolled out since 2023. Fuel prices have risen more than five-fold in Nigeria since the end of a government fuel subsidy scheme, and the naira currency has depreciated by more than 70% in that period, a combination that depresses net incomes both for drivers and transport companies. Some Nigeria analysts have cited a “ challenging macroeconomic environment ” as the root cause of Uber’s exit as more expensive taxis became less preferred to relatively cheaper alternatives like buses, tricycles and motorcycles. Know More InDrive and Estonian company Bolt were Uber’s main Nigeria competitors and are now the main beneficiaries of the latter’s exit. Their ability to tweak parts of their operations to local sensibilities — like InDrive’s bargaining feature, and Bolt’s flexibility with trip cancellation, car models and payment options — diminished the advantages Uber had gained from a two-year headstart, some analysts have argued . Bolt, which pushed into offering three-wheeled taxis outside of Lagos, had won 60% of Nigeria market share by the time of Uber’s exit, Obi said. Active Nigerian users reached 3.3 million last December, more than six times that of Uber , according to Sensor Tower, a California-based app usage tracker. Anburajan agrees with the view that localization may have helped Uber. “Keeping your business model and experience for users and drivers relatively uniform across markets can work if your target riders are international travelers who will place value on an experience that’s the same from one country to the next,” she said. Ride-hailing will remain compelling and competitive in Africa for companies with “an approach that works for locals,” she said. Ultimately, though, size does not equal a large opportunity. The upshot of Obi’s report is that there is simply no scale for Uber to absorb losses that must inevitably result from “a bad combination” of low per-driver volume and a per-ride subsidy. “A platform that has to raise prices by 71% and still needs to subsidize a large share of its rides is in a structural hole it can’t price its way out of.” Room for Disagreement Some analysis of Uber’s exit blames the company for undercutting Nigerian drivers through unilateral fare cuts, prompting the drivers to revolt and port to rivals like Bolt. On the other hand, the exit may be due to a shift in long-term priorities. CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said the 10% cut to the company’s global staff was about “focusing our people and investments against the biggest opportunities ahead of us.” That has been widely interpreted as reflecting Uber’s increasing shift towards self-driving taxis, evidenced by the company’s rollout of 15 robotaxis in London after the headcount cut. It is a line of business that is not yet viable in most African cities due to under-developed road networks and other factors. Notable Uber’s Nigeria exit and overall experience in Africa “undercuts the assumption that U.S. technology companies will inevitably dominate every market they enter,” Onyeka Aralu, a competition fellow at the International Center for Law & Economics in Oregon, argues.

events.title: UAE’s Al Tajir family put Scottish ‘ghost’ golf course up for sale
events.summary: An incomplete golf resort in Scotland, which is owned by a UAE family but has never opened to public, has been put on the market. Located near the world-famous Gleneagles course in Perthshire, gWest was intended to rival the quality of its historic neighbour. But few people have had the chance to play the course on a private gated resort set on an estate spanning more than 80 hectares. It was bought by the UAE’s Al Tajir family in 2007, with the tournament-standard course completed two years later. Mahdi Al Tajir, who in 1971 became the first UAE ambassador to the UK, was named the richest man in Scotland by The Sunday Times in 2013 and owns the Highland Spring water company which is based nearby. But a combination of the financial crisis, the Scottish independence debate and referendum, Brexit and Covid-19 meant the family felt that the time has never been quite right to take it to the next stage of investment. It means the 18th-century-inspired clubhouse remains a shell and plans for the rest of the resort – it has permission for up to 170 residential plots, a hotel and spa, leisure and entertainment facilities and staff accommodation – remain on hold. Offers for the resort are now being welcomed after the family decided to sell up, with property consultant Knight Frank instructed to find a buyer. Euan Kelly, partner at Knight Frank Edinburgh, said: “It is incredibly rare that an opportunity like gWest becomes available. We’re expecting a huge amount of interest from across the globe in what could be a once-in-a-lifetime asset: a substantial consented resort development site, with a golf course designed by a celebrated architect, in one of Scotland’s most prestigious leisure locations. “While the bold ambitions for the site have yet to fully come to fruition, a sale could see them take an important step forward and add another destination to Scotland’s, and Perthshire’s, strong tourist offering.” Celebrated course architect David McLay Kidd designed the championship-standard course and described the resort as “the best inland site I’ve ever seen for a golf course”. It sits in one of Scotland’s best-known golf and leisure corridors, to the west of Gleneagles between Perth and Stirling. The UK’s golf industry generated revenue of around £2.7 billion ($3.64 billion) in 2024/25, which is expected to rise to £3 billion for 2025/26. There are about 560 courses in Scotland – one fifth of the total in the UK. The gWest website says the course has been specifically designed to blend seamlessly with the landscape and enhance the far-reaching views of the surrounding hills and countryside. It says: “The views from the estate are extraordinary, with the Ochil Hills to the south, and to the west, across rolling hills and mountains, Ben Vorlich in Loch Lomond and The Trossachs National Park can be seen. “The estate extends 2.3 miles [3.7km] from east to west and is surrounded by natural land, the majority of which is also owned by the developer, ensuring the boundaries, access and views are protected. Two listed heritage sites of old forts are also located within the grounds of the resort and an ancient church lies just beyond.” Speaking in 2020, Mr Al Tajir’s son, Mohsin, said: “You want to invest. The next phase of gWest is another 50, 60, maybe £100 million. And, as a family, we're not willing to put that sort of money in if we don't know what the future is.” He said with concerns that taxes would go up, rather than becoming a tax haven if independence were to happen, “maybe it's not the place I need to put my money”. He said at the time he had played the course 20 or 30 times, and seemed to suggest he had struggled. He joked that while the course was built by a respected designer, “I’m a bad golfer”.

events.title: The real AI economy is being built by ordinary people
events.summary: Far from Silicon Valley pitch decks, workers across Asia and Africa are bypassing tech industry hype to quietly rewire their daily jobs — one prompt, workflow, and local problem at a time. Rest of World visited workers across Asia and Africa who are using AI to solve daily problems, make a living, and create new possibilities in their everyday lives. These profiles reveal how people choose to leverage artificial intelligence — what they are willing to delegate, which tasks they insist on handling themselves — and how access to cheap, powerful AI can expand the limits of what one person can accomplish. It’s proof the economic impact of AI is taking shape on a personal, local level as forces in Silicon Valley and China battle to command the global AI ecosystem. 🇳🇬 “I have invested my time but not my money” When Nureeyah Ogunmuyiwa decided to hire her first employee earlier this year, she faced an unexpected problem. The 24-year-old makeup artist, who caters to brides and bridal parties among others in Lagos, had never hired anyone before. With her business growing and Ogunmuyiwa stepping into content creation to promote her services, she knew she needed to hire help. But she didn’t know how to write a job description, what questions to ask in an interview, or what qualities to look for in candidates. Within minutes, the chatbot produced a complete hiring plan, including interview questions and a checklist to evaluate candidates. “ChatGPT was my hiring manager that made the process less of a hassle,” Ogunmuyiwa told Rest of World. “I told her that I needed someone reliable, and to let me know what to do and what to look out for. She gave me everything that helped me hire my amazing assistant.” That assistant now works alongside the AI one. Ogunmuyiwa first encountered ChatGPT a couple of years ago while working as a customer support officer at a Lagos logistics startup after graduating from university. She used it to rewrite emails so they sounded more empathetic to customers and professional to colleagues. When she left her job in 2024 to focus full time on the makeup business she had been building on the side since 2018, AI came with her. As a bootstrapped entrepreneur with a small budget, she said ChatGPT has become her “most reliable business partner.” Today, it plays multiple roles. It’s her social media manager, writing captions, suggesting suitable hashtags, and recommending content ideas that have helped attract new customers. It’s her sales coach, helping her refine client pitches so they sound “bold but not too salesy.” It also handles the math. Whenever she restocks beauty products, ChatGPT helps her calculate prices based on costs and profit margins, saving hours of manual calculations. “It saves me from punching each product in the calculator and then trying to do the mental work of arriving at a profitable price point,” Ogunmuyiwa said. Nearly half of Nigeria’s population now has internet access, with the majority connecting through smartphones. Ogunmuyiwa finds the convenience of access to AI bots on her phone very useful. ChatGPT has become one of her most visited apps, alongside WhatsApp Business and Instagram. She prompts it for the simplest tasks like setting reminders. She has organized her conversations with different labels: “Glam by Ree,” named after her business; “return to corporate” for her professional plans; and “my studio project” for creative planning. When Ogunmuyiwa recently moved her business from her dining room to a rented studio, she used AI to generate mood boards, which she shared with carpenters and electricians as they worked on the new space. As new AI tools appeared, she began experimenting beyond ChatGPT. After a friend recommended Anthropic’s Claude earlier this year, she reluctantly gave it a try, worried she’d have to teach another chatbot everything about her business from scratch. Eventually, she settled into using both but highly favors ChatGPT. Ogunmuyiwa recently moved her business into a rented studio and used AI to generate mood boards. Ogunmuyiwa shared AI-generated reference images with carpenters and electricians to design her new studio. Damilare Dosunmu Despite relying on AI throughout her business, Ogunmuyiwa hasn’t paid for either service because she feels the free version serves her purpose. “I have invested my time but not my money,” she said. “And I’m getting a great return.” She is open to a paid version in the future if needed, especially to generate images and mood boards. AI contributes roughly 5% to her business growth. “I can’t give all the credit to AI for giving my business structure because I made a personal decision,” Ogunmuyiwa said. “AI has really helped me to implement that structure in the best way possible. I spent less time on things I trust ChatGPT to handle.” That growing dependence sometimes worries her. At one point, she deliberately stopped using AI because she felt she was consulting it before making every decision.

events.title: Washington's AI paralysis: Let 'er rip vs. hit the brakes
events.summary: President Trump is as all-in on AI as a politician could be: all gas, no brakes, and zero interest in hand-wringing about dystopian risks or public disdain. Democrats are as conflicted on AI as a party could be: skeptical of the labs, spooked by their warnings, but split on whether to shut it all down. Why it matters: This staggering divide makes consensus on federal AI regulation almost unimaginable this year — and probably through early 2029, regardless of who wins control of Congress. Zoom in: Trump has governed as the AI president from Day 1 , applying the same doctrine to models and the data centers that power them — build faster, regulate less, beat China. Speaking in Ireland on Sunday, he dismissed new safety warnings as the work of "a lot of negative forces ... bringing up things that won't happen" — and reduced the stakes to one line: "Whoever wins AI wins." It's unclear which "negative forces" Trump has in mind: Calls to slow the race — or " pace the frontier " — are now coming from the leaders of America's premier AI labs, including Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI and Google. Between the lines: Trump's accelerationist allies, including venture capitalists in Silicon Valley, see the safety alarms as a cynical ploy by the field's dominant players to lock in favorable regulations. David Sacks, Trump's former AI czar and a leading voice for the administration's hands-off approach, has a simple answer : Slow yourselves down. If OpenAI and Anthropic truly think the frontier is moving too fast, Sacks argues, they can decelerate on their own without using Washington to force competitors to do the same. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) echoed Sacks' argument that the labs don't need Congress to slow themselves down — and rejected calls for an emergency moratorium. Johnson said on NBC's "Meet the Press" that he'd recall the House and put AI regulation to a vote "if we had the solution," but warned Congress against rushing into rules it doesn't yet understand. His preferred first step is a summit: Johnson said Sunday he wants Trump, congressional leaders and the heads of the major AI labs in a room as soon as possible to hammer out a common approach to safety. The other side: Congressional Democrats are coalescing around urgency, but have no comparable doctrine on what to actually do. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries says his caucus will meet Tuesday to debate what action to take, while former President Barack Obama is privately urging the party to make AI a top priority. The policy spectrum is vast — and doesn't neatly map onto what the labs themselves are asking for. On the progressive end, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) want to ban superintelligence outright, pause advanced AI development and threaten violators with up to 20 years in prison . Others are reaching for more conventional Washington fixes: Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) wants a bipartisan AI select committee with subpoena power, while Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) is demanding that OpenAI open its models to federal safety reviews. What to watch: The unprecedented push for restraint from inside the AI industry, colliding with deepening public unease, could scramble this political stalemate. Michigan GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers, a Trump ally running in a swing state, said Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's new warning convinced him "we must slow down development" so government can catch up. Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) is investigating AI's "existential risk," while Sens. John Thune (R-S.D.) and Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) are pursuing a narrower plan requiring companies to test and report catastrophic risks. Reality check: Political pressure and lobbying could crack open the door to narrow bipartisan measures, though any meaningful regulation would still have to survive Trump's veto pen. The bottom line: Washington is deeply divided on whether AI is a national triumph to unleash or a national emergency to contain.

events.title: Abu Dhabi's Miral to invest Dh12bn over five years on more Yas Island hotels and attractions
events.summary: Miral , the company behind Yas Island in Abu Dhabi, has announced a Dh12 billion ($3.26 billion) investment over the next five years to expand its hospitality and theme park offerings. The amount will be allocated towards the expansion of a Warner Bros-themed hotel with 250 rooms, as well as a new lifestyle hotel at Yas Bay, Miral's group chief executive Mohamed Al Zaabi said at the Arabian Travel Market in Dubai on Monday. “We want to increase the room number today by almost 35 per cent in the coming five years,” he said. Among the new hotels, two will be based on themed IPs, based on increased demand for such units, he said, without disclosing details of the brands. The investment also encompasses the Harry Potter-themed expansion of its Warner Bros theme park, set to open in 2029. New rides in Ferrari World, Warner Bros and other new experiences will also be revealed as part of the expansion plans, Mr Al Zaabi said. The investment will be sourced mainly from Miral's earnings. “There will be a percentage that will be financed and we will try to use our resources to fund those projects,” he said. Disneyland Abu Dhabi Mr Al Zaabi also confirmed that progress on the new Disneyland Abu Dhabi theme park, which is not part of the Dh12 billion investment pipeline, is proceeding. “I'm very happy with the progress … we work hand in hand with Disney and we meet them literally every month,” he said. He did not reveal any dates for the opening of the theme park, which is also set to come up on Yas Island. Miral said its investment in new projects will support job creation and skills development in the tourism sector while enhancing Abu Dhabi's tourism experience. The investment signals a commitment to Abu Dhabi’s long-term tourism, Mohamed Al Mubarak, chairman of Miral, said in a statement. “Yas Island has become a global success story, demonstrating how world class experiences contribute to economic growth, enhance quality of life, and strengthen Abu Dhabi’s appeal to audiences from around the world.” Abu Dhabi’s Tourism Strategy 2030 plans to boost visitor numbers to 39.3 million, increase the sector's GDP contribution to Dh90 billion and create 178,000 new jobs within the tourism ecosystem. Mr Al Zaabi said: “We are not competing regionally, we are competing internationally. Tourists in India, China, any tourist market, the first thing they see [when researching destinations] is their mobile phone. [People have] worldwide access, so you are head to head with Paris, you are head to head with London, New York, Orlando.” The key is to stand out and having indoor theme parks makes the emirate a unique summertime destination, he added. Miral did not close any of its theme parks during the Iran conflict. Occupancy levels at the hotels on Yas Island were supported by staycation guests, he said. “Since June, we have seen a positive trend,” Mr Al Zaabi said. Along with the UAE market, they have been receiving visitors from the Gulf, India and Russia. “In general, I see a positive trend and we are very optimistic about the coming months as well,” he said. “I think next year will be a very good year for us.” Arabian Travel Market in pictures

events.title: Etihad expects 2026 break-even and strong demand despite Iran war
events.summary: Etihad Airways expects to break even this year due to strong demand despite the Iran war, reversing a forecast in June that it could post an annual loss. The Abu Dhabi airline is flying with planes 90 per cent full, generating positive cash flow and benefitting from a “booming” air cargo business, chief executive Antonoaldo Neves told The National on Monday at the Arabian Travel Market. The airline added 15 per cent capacity in July year-on-year, recorded a profit in August and held air fares at the same rate as last year despite an increase in jet fuel prices. "We are breaking even this year. We are not budgeting for a loss this year. We see demand very, very strong," he said. This comes after Etihad posted record annual profit after tax of Dh2.6 billion ($707.9 million) in 2025, up 47 per cent on 2024. In June, Mr Neves said the airline was unlikely to make a profit or may break even depending on the second half of the year. The prediction came as the Iran war disrupted regional air travel, leading to longer routes and higher jet fuel prices. Mr Neves said the airline was only one to two per cent behind its budget for the year, with growth of 15 per cent in Available Seat Kilometres (ASKs), a measure of its total passenger-carrying capacity, compared with the original target of 18 per cent. Etihad is "doubling the bet" as it continues to buy planes, hire talent and invest in new products, he said. The airline currently operates 320 flights a day, which it plans to increase by 25 per cent by the end of next year to about 400 flights, he added. Etihad had undergone years of restructuring before it returned to annual net profitability in 2022, ending a streak of losses that began in 2016. Asked whether the regional crisis would exert pressure on the airline's achievements, Mr Neves said: "This situation was a great test for Etihad ... we passed the test." He referred to the airline's ongoing investments in people and products, a strong balance sheet and continued cash generation this year. "We have the ability to absorb the crisis. If this was before 2019, we'd be going to cost-cutting mode," he said, referring to the airline's restructuring phase. "The model was tested, and the model response was the right one. We're confident about keeping investing. Things are going to improve and have been improving." Next wave of growth The next wave of growth next year will come from markets in China and Africa, with a focus on Latin America in 2028 or 2029, Mr Neves added. The airline has been adding an average of 20 destinations per year over the last couple of years in a burst of rapid growth, taking it to about 120 destinations currently. The lastest announcement is a flight to Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast from October 4. Etihad has a list of 10 priority countries in which it is pursuing airport slots or traffic rights, including to the island nation of Mauritius, South East Asia, Middle East and Europe, he said. events.title: How Republicans secretly got Fetterman for their convention
events.summary: The biggest surprise of last week's Republican midterm convention began with an audacious request from the organizers to GOP Sen. Dave McCormick: Could he get Democratic Sen. John Fetterman, a fellow Pennsylvanian, to make an appearance? "I'll ask him," McCormick said. Within days, Fetterman — who's been increasingly at odds with the Democratic Party's liberal wing — was on board. Why it matters: Fetterman's 64-second video — calling himself a "common-sense Democrat," praising McCormick and vowing to work with President Trump to defend Pennsylvania's steel industry — represented Fetterman's biggest break yet with his party. Behind the scenes: According to three sources familiar with the talks, the idea for Fetterman to make the appearance emerged over the summer, as organizers of the Dallas convention sought what they called an "Oh sh*t" moment. They were looking to drive home a key midterm message — that Democrats are too extreme. Organizers discussed featuring "walk away" figures — people who had supported Democrats but had become disillusioned with the party. Republican operative Tony Sayegh, a leading convention organizer, was a driving force behind the idea, and Trump adviser Jason Miller backed the plan. Fetterman topped their list. Zoom in: Sayegh, a friend of McCormick's, took the idea to him in July. McCormick had developed a friendship with Fetterman as the Democrat grew more estranged from his party, particularly over many Democrats' criticism of Israel. Organizers knew getting Fetterman involved would be a massive coup. The intrigue: McCormick approached Fetterman carefully, knowing the backlash his Democratic colleague could face if he agreed to a role in the GOP convention. McCormick asked Fetterman to introduce him at the convention. A source said McCormick added: "I don't want you to do something that's not good for you." The two senators hashed it out over calls and texts for a few days. "I want to do it. I'm sure it will make people mad," Fetterman told McCormick, according to the source. "But you're my friend, and I want to introduce you." Fetterman's decision was driven by his friendship with McCormick, not a desire to help Republicans , said a source familiar with his thinking. Fetterman "had no interest in being a pawn in a larger Republican play," the source said. There was brief talk of Fetterman traveling to Dallas to introduce McCormick in person, but he decided against it. Instead, Fetterman proposed recording a video outside a steel mill near his home in Braddock, Pa. McCormick's team arranged for a videographer to meet him there. Fetterman didn't use a script. He riffed in front of the camera. He focused on introducing McCormick and highlighting their bipartisan work in support of Pennsylvania's steel industry. Neither McCormick nor convention organizers tried to alter what he said. The notion of Fetterman switching parties never came up, according to a source familiar with the deliberations. Organizers saw Fetterman's appearance as a jolt that would draw eyeballs to the first-of-its-kind midterm convention — and play big on social media. To preserve the surprise, organizers kept the circle tight. McCormick looped in his chief of staff, Mark Isakowitz, and only a few others. Miller was Sayegh's point of contact in the White House. Fetterman went even further: He told no one on his team, a source told Axios. The bottom line: Fetterman's appearance at Trump's convention deepened his estrangement from the Democratic Party. But Fetterman reiterated after his appearance that he isn't switching parties, calling himself a "lifelong Democrat" and saying that if Democrats win control of the Senate in November, he'd remain the "51st vote."

events.title: Researchers probe how Democrats could win working-class voters
events.summary: Democrats need to employ more populist rhetoric, run candidates perceived as non-elite, and steer away from progressive rhetoric like “abolish ICE” if they want to capture more working-class voters in future elections, according to new data shared first with Semafor. Researchers at the Center for Working-Class Politics talked to 40,000 adults from April to June to determine how Democrats can win more working-class voters without compromising other support. The strategy should also include leading with “working-class economics” and explicitly prioritizing members of the working class, the research found. Working-class voters moved away from Democrats if the candidates endorsed defunding police (by 5.7 points), letting transgender girls play girls sports (by 5.6 points), or gun control (4 points). These voters were interested in economic populism, but a candidate’s background couldn’t overwhelm cultural concerns: On those, said Jared Abbott, the center’s director, “it’s better for you to say something that actually connects with those voters and that you agree with than to say nothing.”

events.title: ‘I Like My Big Rat Wife’: Meet the People Using Chatbots to Write Custom Fiction
events.summary: When Petra Ferraz de Novaes isn’t at work, she’s probably lost in a fantasy crafted with the help of artificial intelligence . Novaes, a 36-year-old software engineer from Brazil, has always loved storytelling. But making every little decision that goes into it—from style and syntax to character development—felt impossible. So in 2024 she asked an AI model to bring one of her ideas to life. Novaes was delighted by the eccentric, sometimes wayward interpretations of her prompts, which carried the narrative in unexpected directions. “What fascinates me is the unpredictability,” Novaes tells WIRED. “People say that AI hallucinates a lot. But in this case, it’s probably what you want.” These days, Novaes spends hours at a time building stories with AI, using a program called SillyTavern to run open-source models on her computer. She sketches out a concept—an elven warrior battles the queen of the Amazons and seizes her throne, for example—and watches the model fill in the gaps. In a single session, Novaes switches between multiple fantasy worlds. Some are hers, and others she borrows—she likes Star Wars , Pokémon, and Mass Effect . Sometimes, Novaes works up self-contained stories the length of a small novel, which she might share online . Otherwise, she participates in private role-plays. “It can be never-ending. You find a quest, you complete it, you go for the next one,” says Novaes. “The limit is your imagination.” According to a recent study , plenty of people share Novaes’ hobby. “They know [the stories are] produced by an AI model, and they don’t care,” says Melanie Walsh, an assistant professor at the University of Washington Information School who coauthored the study. “In fact, that seems to be a big part of the attraction.” Lately, the publishing industry has suffered a series of scandals involving the suspected use of AI by professional authors. One publisher canceled a $2 million book deal; another withdrew a novel from the shelves; readers alleged that a prize-winning short story was AI-generated. Implicit in all of these incidents is the idea that nobody wants to read stories generated by machine—that using AI to craft fiction devalues the art form. But the commotion has distracted from the behavior of readers, Walsh and her colleagues argue, and what it might signal about the appetite for AI fiction. Analyzing more than 500,000 prompts fed into ChatGPT, drawn from a public dataset called WildChat, the researchers found that more than a third of chatbot interactions involve some form of fiction generation, including prose and poetry, fan fiction, erotica, or role-play. The vast majority of fiction prompts, the researchers found, stem from a small collection of “power users” who generate and tweak stories obsessively. In one case, a single user prompted ChatGPT to generate versions of the same fan-fiction narrative—set in the world of anime video game Doki Doki Literature Club !—thousands of times over the course of several months. But even controlling for heavy use, the researchers estimate that 7 percent of chatbot users engage in fiction generation. The WildChat dataset has its limitations. Because the prompts are anonymized, it’s impossible to capture any demographic data. Participants also had to agree to make their prompts public, meaning the group may not reflect the population at large; OpenAI told WIRED that “WildChat is not a representative sample of all ChatGPT users.” A 2025 study by OpenAI and the National Bureau of Economic Research suggests that 1.4 percent of ChatGPT prompts are fiction-related, a long way short of the researchers’ estimate. (OpenAI’s figure does not include role-play; the company could not confirm whether it counts erotica.) Still, Walsh and her colleagues argue it’s clear that a committed subsection of readers are generating custom, personal fiction. The researchers believe that some people are drawn to the ability to repeatedly and rapidly iterate on a story, while others value the chance to direct the action, no longer hemmed in by an author’s decisions. “There are a lot of qualities of AI models that are different from what human writers have that are actually appealing to at least some segment of users,” says Walsh. “These models are judgment-free; they can produce stories instantaneously; they are nearly inexhaustible.” For erotica fans, AI creates an opportunity to insert themselves into the action and converse with the characters they cook up. “It’s a digital choose-your-own-adventure book but with infinite swipes,” says Razrien, a 40-year-old man from Indiana who asked to appear under his online username to speak frankly about his sexual kinks. Razrien uses AI to create fantasy characters who dominate him in role-play: a “big angry rat wife” and an “eight-foot tall werewolf mommy with a bad temper,” among others. He has learned which models are best able to satisfy certain kinks; Google’s Gemma 4 is his current all-around favorite.

events.title: Klomp, nominated for No. 2 health post, faces Senate gauntlet
events.summary: Democrats want to cast Chris Klomp as anything but a moderating force within Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Department of Health and Human Services this week during two Senate hearings on his nomination to become Kennedy’s No. 2. But the genial official — who won the trust of the White House negotiating Trump’s drug pricing deals and playing a key role reshaping leadership teams across HHS — has quietly met with nearly 35 senators ahead of his confirmation hearings before the Senate finance and health panels, according to a person familiar with the outreach. A Democratic aide said that progressives would try to use the hearings to dispel what they see as a false narrative that Klomp is a bridge-builder who was elevated at the behest of the White House to restrain Kennedy’s anti-vaccine impulses. But while Klomp is unlikely to draw public support from Democrats, behind closed doors, many lawmakers view him as one of President Donald Trump’s most competent health officials.

events.title: Fed poised to clash with Trump
events.summary: As the Federal Reserve weighs whether to raise interest rates this week, Chair Kevin Warsh must choose between breaking markets’ trust and triggering President Donald Trump’s ire. Vice President JD Vance and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recently joined the president in arguing for lower interest rates. But investors overwhelmingly expect Warsh to deliver on his hawkish speech in Jackson Hole last month. Disappointing them would hurt his credibility, particularly after the government said that prices beyond food and energy rose more in August than expected. The damage could be severe enough to boost borrowing costs even in the absence of a hike. “Warsh’s Jackson Hole speech led the market to expect a hike if the inflation news was imperfect, and while the [consumer price index] was not concerning, it was imperfect,” Goldman Sachs analysts wrote. Officials “might worry about the consequences of not hiking for market perceptions.” — Eleanor Mueller

events.title: House Democrat pushes global effort on AI rules
events.summary: House Democrats are circulating a letter imploring President Donald Trump to lead an international effort to set global AI rules, according to a copy shared with Semafor. “We strongly urge your administration to lead a coordinated international effort to establish a global framework to guide the development of this technology and a shared vision for AI end-use — engaging our strongest allies, such as the European Union, as well as formidable global competitors, particularly the People’s Republic of China,” Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., writes in the draft of the letter to be sent later this week. It’s unclear which other lawmakers will sign on. The push precedes President Donald Trump’s meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping, which will touch on AI. Panic over AI’s capabilities is also rising among lawmakers and the American public. “We must lead with the creation of global rules of the road to prevent the proliferation of uncontrollable highly capable frontier AI,” the letter reads, comparing the push to past US-led efforts on nuclear power and aviation. The US has been very clear about its desire to lead China in AI development, and it’s unlikely that the Trump administration would play any role in international policy decisions about AI that would involve ceding competitive ground. On Sunday, Trump rejected calls by tech leaders for a slowdown in AI development, citing the need for the US to outcompete China. The White House has often opted out of global discussions about AI; last year, White House science adviser Michael Kratsios said at the UN: “We totally reject all efforts by international bodies to assert centralized control and global governance of AI.” It’s still possible the rapid pace of AI development will shift the administration’s approach. Trump’s talks with Xi on AI, and the upcoming UN General Assembly, will present a chance to test whether his administration has altered course at all.

events.title: Republicans’ time crunch: Data centers, sports, crypto
events.summary: The News Some Republicans are hoping they can address voters’ affordability concerns before the election — potentially by passing a data center power bill to demonstrate the party is listening to souring popular sentiment surrounding AI infrastructure. The House is set to take up the bill, called the Ratepayer Protection Act, this week, which will help vulnerable incumbents answer voters’ concerns about data centers. If the Senate takes it up, the bill would help endangered Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio. But the body has other priorities: The Senate is scheduled to take up the crypto market structure bill and a huge bipartisan college sports bill as soon as this week. There’s a faction of Republicans who’d rather concentrate on deregulatory rollbacks and addressing AI’s impact on utility bills; Republicans will try and sort it out this week in party meetings. Know More Most Senate denizens expect Tuesday’s crypto bill to fail given the standoff over new ethics rules governing President Donald Trump and his family. The Protect College Sports Act has better prospects and could receive a vote as early as this week. Members of both parties are optimistic about the college sports bill despite Democrats’ filibuster leverage, and one of the bill’s wealthy benefactors is trying to make sure it stays front and center. Saving College Sports, a group founded by Texas Tech University System Board of Regents Chair Cody Campbell, is spending an additional $300,000 on ads between Monday and Tuesday on programs watched closely by lawmakers, including on Fox News, MS NOW and CNN, according to a person familiar with the plans. If the bill advances on the Senate floor, it could take a significant amount of time to process — especially if there’s a protracted amendment fight. That would threaten to eat into the limited three-week work session before the midterm elections, limiting other legislative action; Senate Republicans also wanted to confirm Trump’s judicial nominees and Keith Sonderling, his new pick for Labor secretary. Senate Republicans are also coordinating with the House about deregulatory rollbacks they might be able to accomplish this month. The House is scheduled to take up two California environmental disapproval resolutions this week — members’ last week in town before they break ahead of the midterms. By taking the lead on the data center power bill, House Republicans could provide some political cover for that bill’s sponsor, purple-district Rep. Gabe Evans, R-Colo. The House is also set to vote on a Senate-passed bill named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., that would ratchet up pressure on Russia by penalizing its trading partners, though many House Democrats are expected to oppose it because of concerns about handing over more tariff authority to Trump.

events.title: AI risk warnings belie lack of consensus in Congress
events.summary: The sudden appearance of alignment among AI CEOs about industry regulation over the weekend masks an inconvenient reality for Congress: There is no consensus. In the House, Speaker Mike Johnson is downplaying his own role in favor of a “partnership” with AI companies, as he told CNN on Sunday. Across the Capitol, OpenAI remains most supportive of bipartisan Senate Commerce Committee talks that could advance this week, despite skepticism from Anthropic, Democrats, and AI safety groups, who say those negotiations risk letting the industry self-police. But Saturday’s three-CEO agreement that frontier models are accelerating too fast centered on Anthropic’s plan to do “things every AI lab needs to do anyway,” as our colleague Reed Albergotti wrote — which amounts to self-regulation, with labs likely choosing their own independent evaluators. “The time to act is now, before it’s too late,” Rep. Lori Trahan, D-Mass., told Semafor. She urged Johnson to keep the House in session past this week to work on AI, but her own leader is already looking to 2027. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries told ABC on Sunday that his caucus would gather this week to discuss options. At a separate closed-door fireside chat with Jeffries last week, former President Barack Obama urged the New Yorker to “put together a framework for a very public conversation” and said he’d prioritize the issue if he were running for president, according to excerpts of the remarks confirmed by Obama’s office. — Ashley Gold and Nicholas Wu

They have also been accused of fraudulently relabelling frozen meat products to alter production and best before dates. The Wilsons are to return to court in coming weeks. A Queensland pork industry heavyweight has been named as one of the people charged over alleged large-scale financial crimes that authorities claim resulted in tens of millions of dollars being funnelled out of businesses for personal use. Darren Gary Wilson, 63, alongside Cameron Ronald Wilson are alleged to have kept $10 million in sales records off the books for personal use and moved more than $30 million in cash between New South Wales and Queensland between 2017 and 2026. The men are facing multiple charges each including receiving and possessing tainted property, destroying records, fraud, making false declarations and fraudulent omission of entry in record. Pork industry financial crimes charges Police allege about $10 million was funnelled out of businesses in the pork meat industry for personal use. Authorities have confirmed the changes did not pose a risk to food safety. The pair were not required to appear in person on Monday and their bail has been extended. Darren Wilson is a prominent face in the pork industry, starting Wilpak wholesale meats in Ipswich in the 1980s. The company has since expanded to include meat processing and pig farms in Queensland. He is also widely known in the racing industry. Darren and Cameron Wilson are to return to court in coming weeks. The pair were charged following a joint investigation involving the Queensland Crime and Corruption Commission, the New South Wales Police Anti-Money Laundering Unit and the New South Wales Crime Commission. events.title: Heading off to uni? Here's what to insure against theft
events.summary: Laptops, phones and bikes are top of the shopping list for thieves as students head off to university, according to insurer Aviva. They are the items most likely to be on student insurance claims - after being stolen from digs, cars, public transport and bars and restaurants. But there are ways you can help keep them safe, and things to consider if you are planning to get insurance cover. Get it wrong and it can be expensive, or possibly illegal. The majority of student insurance claims are the result of theft, ahead of accidental damage, according to Aviva. The insurer declined to say what proportion of claims resulted in payouts. "Laptops, computers and mobile phones play a vital role in student life, but they can also be attractive targets for opportunistic thieves due to their value and portability," said Steven Jackson, its home product manager. Leaving really expensive and sentimental belongings back at home Locking up valuables and keeping them out of sight when you're out Staying vigilant - do you really need to leave your bag or laptop to reserve a café table or a spot in the library? It is entirely the choice of an individual as to whether it is worth insuring belongings while off at university or college. Car insurance is compulsory, says the Association of British Insurers (ABI), but you can choose whether it's worth insuring your bike or other items. How to make sure you've got the correct cover First, the ABI suggests checking if you are covered already. Some student halls might already include insurance, or your parents' policy might extend to you. If not, there is the option of buying contents insurance. "This type of policy covers the cost of replacing or repairing your possessions if they are damaged, destroyed or stolen - giving you peace of mind that you're protected should something go wrong," the ABI said. You must check how much you're covered for and whether it's enough to replace everything, including the maximum value of a claim on a single item. You can do this by creating an inventory of all of your contents, including clothes, electronics and furniture, and adding up the cost of replacing each item. You might need to pay extra to cover a nice bike, or to cover items that you take out and about with you rather than leave in your accommodation. And, if you're driving, make sure your insurer knows the car is kept somewhere new. If it is your parents' car and you are now the main driver, you have to inform the insurer. It's illegal if you don't. Are you starting university soon? Share your thoughts. events.title: MPs and Lords call for new law to address AI threat to human rights
events.summary: A cross-party group of MPs and peers has identified human rights risks posed by artificial intelligence (AI), arguing existing laws are ill-equipped to address the technology's rapid growth. The Joint Committee on Human Rights (JCHR) published a report calling for a new bill on AI to "address the scale and seriousness" of such threats. "Nowhere in the world, including the UK, has a current legislative and regulatory approach to AI that is fit for purpose," said Labour MP and committee chair Alex Sobel. Labour education minister Georgia Gould said AI was creating opportunities but that it was critical the government was "responding to those risks" posed by the technology. In a summary of its 100-page report, the JCHR argued AI has been responsible for numerous abuses of human rights, citing examples including the use of AI to create sexualised images of women and girls, and scanning people's faces without their consent. The JCHR has advocated for the creation of a "single, independent AI oversight body... on a statutory basis", saying the current legal framework is "fragmented and difficult to navigate", "leaving gaps in protection". The report goes on to call for "more demanding obligations for higher risk AI systems and models" at all stages of the "AI lifecycle". It continues: "Some uses of AI should be prohibited outright because they are incompatible with human rights. Potential areas for action include subliminal techniques, and inappropriate use of profiling or biometric data." The committee's chair said: "AI is heralded as an unprecedented era of technological development with the potential to transform our lives for better or for worse." "It is moving with such speed and complexity that its impact is hard to accurately predict. What is clear is that at present we are unprepared to deal with its consequences however potentially dire they may be." The JCHR's 12 members are drawn from both Houses of Parliament and they currently include MPs and peers from the Labour, Conservative and Liberal Democrat parties. Monday's report comes amid growing anxiety over the challenges posed by AI. Jacob Coxon, an AI researcher who quit Anthropic, told the BBC this weekend that staff developing the systems were "genuinely frightened" for the future of humanity . An Anthropic spokesperson told BBC News that it was building "models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry". Labour's 2024 general election manifesto said it would "ensure the safe development and use of AI models by introducing binding regulation on the handful of companies developing the most powerful AI models". The government used the King's Speech in July 2024 to commit to bringing forward "appropriate legislation", but no dedicated AI bill appeared in this year's King's Speech. Asked what had happened to the law promised by Labour, Gould told BBC Breakfast that the government "has been regulating" - including action to tackle non-consensual sexualised deepfakes and a bill linked to cyber security. She said: "There is action happening and we're continuing to really carefully monitor the rise of AI, the way the technology is evolving and making sure we're staying alongside it, and we have some of the best people in the world doing that work." Gould said the AI Security Institute was "working through challenges coming in the future, testing models when they're coming into the UK", and that there was a need to work with other countries on the issue. Following his arrival in No 10 in July, Prime Minister Andy Burnham ensured AI Minister Kanishka Narayan would attend cabinet meetings after scrapping the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology and splitting its responsibilities among other government departments. On Saturday, the head of Anthropic, Dario Amodei, proposed a plan calling for the regulation of AI. Amodei's plan included global regulation, industry-wide regulation and independent monitoring of AI models as they are developed. He also urged the pace of development to be slowed down and the bosses of two rival AI firms, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk, said they agreed with him. One human rights concern raised in recent years is that AI can display biases against particular groups if trained on large datasets scraped from the internet which can include racist, sexist and other undesirable material. AI could also be used to create and spread misinformation. events.title: Advanced Packaging Changes The Rules For Semiconductor Health And Performance Management
events.summary: Systems-in-Package (SiPs) are enabling the next generation of Agentic and Physical AI across cloud, telecommunications, mobile, automotive and high-performance computing platforms. As infrastructure evolves from monolithic devices toward heterogeneous architectures, advanced packaging is becoming increasingly critical to achieving the required performance, bandwidth and power efficiency. But as processors, accelerators, memory and connectivity are brought together through increasingly sophisticated multi-die packages, managing each component in isolation is no longer enough. A SiP is not simply a collection of individual dies. Once chiplets are integrated into the same package, new interactions emerge between them and with the package itself. Understanding those interactions requires visibility not only into each individual chiplet, but into how the chiplets behave together as a system. Why a SiP is harder than the sum of its dies Advanced packaging enables semiconductor companies to integrate more dies and increasingly heterogeneous components using technologies such as interposers, advanced substrates, through-silicon vias (TSVs), die stacking and high-bandwidth memory (HBM). These architectures provide enormous benefits, but they also introduce new electrical, thermal and mechanical interactions. Challenges of systems-in-package. Power delivery becomes a system-level challenge. Different chiplets can have very different power demands, and activity on one die can influence the operating margins of another. IR drop, simultaneous switching noise, fast transients and shared power delivery networks can create voltage behavior that cannot be understood by looking at each chiplet independently. Thermal behavior becomes increasingly coupled. High-power compute dies, HBM and other components are placed in close proximity, creating hotspots, thermal gradients and heat transfer between neighboring dies. In 3D architectures, heat removal becomes even more difficult as dies are vertically stacked and thermal paths become constrained. Mechanical effects can become electrical effects. Warpage, package stress and thermo-mechanical effects introduced during assembly can alter timing and voltage margins. A die that behaved one way at wafer sort may behave differently after it has been bonded, stacked or integrated into the final package. Yield economics become more challenging. A marginal die discovered at wafer sort is one problem. Discovering that same die after it has been integrated with an expensive interposer, substrate, HBM and other known-good components is a much more costly problem. Compound yield therefore becomes increasingly important as the number and value of components within the package increase. And observability becomes harder just when it becomes more important. Once dies are assembled into a package, traditional probing becomes limited, fault isolation becomes more difficult and determining whether a problem originated in a chiplet, an interface, the package or an interaction between components can require significant debug effort. Quality becomes harder to measure and assure. Advanced packaging introduces thousands of critical connections, including micro-bumps and other package interconnects, whose quality can be difficult to characterize directly. Marginal connections may pass conventional production tests yet contribute to degradation or failures later in the product lifecycle. When a system fails in production or returns from the field, determining whether the root cause lies in the chiplets, an interconnect or the package itself can be extremely difficult. This creates a need for measurable indicators of quality that can help identify marginalities early and track degradation over time. Power delivery is one important example. As power traverses increasingly complex package structures and interconnects, and as the current density over these structures is ever increasing, the quality of the power-delivery path can directly affect voltage margin and system behavior. Different chiplets can have very different power demands, while IR drop, simultaneous switching noise, fast transients and shared power delivery networks can create effects that cannot be understood by looking at each chiplet independently. Even though power delivery is distributed over thousands of bumps, pads and through silicon vias (TSVs), a degradation of even one of them may cause a domino effect causing faster degradation of the neighboring pads. The challenge is amplified further as the industry moves toward heterogeneous, multi-vendor chiplet ecosystems. No single die tells the whole story – and no single chiplet vendor necessarily has visibility into the complete package. Shift left: Know more before you package The economics of advanced packaging make early decisions particularly valuable. Conventional pass/fail testing at wafer sort may not reveal the parametric marginalities that become important after integration. For advanced packaging, that may not be enough. A die can pass conventional tests and still carry parametric marginalities that become important only after packaging. Deep in-die measurements can provide another layer of information: how much timing margin exists, how a die responds to voltage variation, whether its parametric signature differs from its population and whether its behavior indicates increased sensitivity to the conditions it will experience after assembly. This enables manufacturers to shift critical decisions left, before committing a die to an increasingly valuable package. For example, telemetry-based advanced analytics and parametric deep data at wafer sort enable outlier detection beyond the industry’s best known methods, per-chiplet VDDmin prediction for static Voperational setting, and power/performance grading for chiplet mix-and-match. These insights can increase confidence in known-good-die quality and help prevent marginal dies from progressing into expensive downstream assembly. Advanced telemetry-based analytics for shift-left SiP production testing. The objective is no longer simply Known Good Die . It is increasingly: Is this die ready to become part of this SiP? That distinction can have a significant impact on compound yield, package scrap cost and final product quality. What changed throughout packaging? Pre-packaging visibility is only one side of the problem. Once a die has been integrated, manufacturers need to understand what has changed. This is where pre-to-post packaging correlation becomes particularly valuable. By comparing parametric behavior before and after integration, changes associated with packaging can be identified and quantified. A shift in timing margin, for example, may indicate an integration-induced effect rather than an intrinsic silicon defect. Changes in voltage behavior may point toward package power delivery. events.title: Asian Captive Conference 2026 Highlights How Captives Are Utilised as Businesses Navigate Risks
events.summary: 8th Asian Captive Conference convened regulators, industry leaders and risk professionals to discuss developments and the future of global captive insurance [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] KUALA LUMPUR, 11 September 2026 — The 8th Asian Captive Conference (ACC) 2026 yesterday brought together more than 300 risk and industry professionals from the region and beyond to explore how captive insurance is enabling businesses to refine their risk management strategy amid an uncertain and multi-faceted operating environment. The conference was co-organised by Labuan IBFC Incorporated Sdn. Bhd. (Labuan IBFC Inc.) and the Labuan International Insurance Association (LIIA). The conference highlighted the growing role of captives in strengthening resilience, enhancing risk-financing control and addressing emerging risks. This growing interest was reflected in the diverse delegate profile, spanning regulators, multinational corporations, and representatives from the captive insurance ecosystem, underscoring the increasing recognition of captive insurance as a strategic risk-financing solution. The conference opened with a welcome address by Ben Quah, CEO of Labuan IBFC Inc., who noted the growing recognition of captives as a strategic tool for managing complex risks. “A captive is no longer simply an alternative mechanism for financing predictable or difficult-to-place risks. Increasingly, it is becoming a strategic instrument that enables organisations to understand their risks more deeply, respond with greater flexibility and retain greater control over how those risks are financed,” he said. This was followed by a keynote address by Affendi Rashdi, Director-General of the Labuan Financial Services Authority (Labuan FSA), who highlighted the evolving role of captives in addressing increasingly complex risks and strengthening resilience. “We may not be able to eliminate volatility, but we can be better prepared for it. Volatility may be unavoidable - but vulnerability does not have to be,” he elaborated. The conference witnessed the launch of the LIIA Women in Captive Insurance, Asia’s first dedicated industry network for women in the captive insurance sector. The initiative aims to advance female talent through mentorship, leadership development and cross-border knowledge exchange, with Affendi Rashdi, Director-General of the Labuan FSA, named as its inaugural Male Ally Champion. The flagship panel, “Unlocking Captive Potential: Regulatory Perspectives from Asia and Emerging Markets,” comprising regulators from Labuan IBFC, Hong Kong and Singapore, reinforced the importance of closer regional engagement and continued alignment between regulators and industry stakeholders to support the sustainable growth of captive markets across Asia. ACC 2026 also featured an industry dialogue with experts from Labuan IBFC, China and Hong Kong which highlighted the increasing relevance of captive structures for Chinese businesses expanding internationally, particularly as companies seek greater control and diversification in managing cross-border and emerging risks. The afternoon programme explored developments in captive takaful, employee benefits captives and emerging technologies, highlighting new opportunities for organisations to enhance risk management, efficiency and tailor their risk-financing strategies beyond traditional property and casualty applications. The conference concluded with an executive panel exploring how captives and parametric insurance can complement traditional programmes to address climate, energy transition and other emerging risks, providing greater flexibility and resilience in risk financing. Annie Undikai, Chairwoman of LIIA, delivered the closing remarks and underscored the importance of people and collaboration in shaping a stronger captive insurance industry. “Capital builds captives, but people, ideas, and relationships shape the future of captive insurance,” she commented. The 8th Asian Captive Conference reaffirmed the importance of continued regulatory dialogue, industry collaboration and innovation in strengthening Asia’s captive insurance ecosystem. As organisations face increasingly interconnected and unpredictable risks, captives are emerging as an increasingly strategic tool for building resilience and developing more responsive and sustainable risk-financing strategies.

events.title: Citi raised more than $40 billion for Saudi clients this year
events.summary: The Scoop Citigroup has raised more than $40 billion to support Saudi clients so far this year, and increased its direct exposure to the kingdom since the Iran war began, maintaining its bet on the kingdom as a key growth market. The US bank has decided to boost internal exposure limits because Saudi Arabia has demonstrated “strong economic resilience and financial resilience,” Citi’s chief country officer for Saudi Arabia, Fahad Aldeweesh, told Semafor in an interview. Saudi Arabia remains a “high priority market for Citi,” with room to grow despite disruptions caused by more than six months of conflict in the region and Iran’s attempts to shut down shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Under CEO Jane Fraser, Citi has made Saudi Arabia a key part of its growth plans, establishing a regional headquarters in Riyadh last year and aggressively pursuing mandates on deals across initial public offerings, merger and acquisitions, and debt financings. Fraser was named co-chair of the US-Saudi Business Council last year. Citi also acted as one of the global coordinators on Saudi Arabia’s $3.25 billion islamic bond sale earlier this month, and is reportedly advising Aramco on a potential sale of a stake in its oil export and storage terminals. “It’s very helpful for our efforts on the ground to support clients here at this time and also to show confidence in the prospects of the country region during this period,” Aldeweesh said, declining to comment on specific transactions. Know More Citi has been working on boosting its Saudi footprint for several years. Although it first entered the kingdom in 1955 when it was the first US bank to operate there, it sold a stake in one of Saudi’s largest banks in 2004, ending its on-the-ground presence. It returned in 2017 with an investment banking license as Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman embarked on an economic overhaul that attracted Wall Street’s biggest names, tempted by fees on government debt sales, Aramco’s IPO, and international acquisitions by the kingdom’s sovereign wealth fund. Saudi Arabia is expected to be a strong driver for investment banking deals in coming years as it sells more debt and seeks foreign investors. Public Investment Fund has made attracting third-party capital to help fund its economic transformation projects as a pillar of its new five-year strategy and recently sent executives to New York to drum up interest from potential investors, Semafor reported last week. Courtesy of Citi International private equity and infrastructure investors are showing greater interest in the kingdom, Aldeweesh said. “We see them actively looking for opportunities and also hoping additional deal flow would be made available to them,” he said. Foreign stock market investors have added $3 billion to their Saudi holdings since the start of the year, he added, boosting Citi’s trading and custody business. Citi has a “strong” transaction pipeline in the works and is optimistic that IPO activity will pick up in coming months, Aldeweesh added. The bank employs around 35 staff in Saudi Arabia and plans to keep hiring, he said, declining to specify how many will be recruited. Notable Citi opened its regional headquarters in Riyadh last year, signalling a commitment from the US bank to join peers seeking to establish a stronger foothold with the government and PIF, Bloomberg reported in October.
